title: The 'Null Key' Skew Trap in Inner and Left Joins
scenario: A transactional lakehouse joins an incoming fact table of 200 million web events with a users dimension table. However, 30% of the incoming events are from unauthenticated guest users where `user_id` is NULL. During the shuffle phase of a SortMergeJoin, the stage reaches 199/200 tasks in 45 seconds, while the final task (Task 200) hangs for 35 minutes before failing with an executor timeout.
symptom: Spark UI shows 199 tasks completed with ~5MB shuffle read each, but 1 task processed 45GB shuffle read with massive Tungsten disk spill and eventual `ExecutorLostFailure (heartbeat timed out)`.
root_cause: Hash partitioning computes `Murmur3Hash(null) % numPartitions = 0` (or a single fixed partition ID). Consequently, all 60 million records with `user_id IS NULL` are routed to the exact same reducer task, overwhelming that single core.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
events_df = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/events/") # 200M rows, 30% NULL user_id
users_df = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/users/")

# Unsanitized Join on nullable foreign key
joined_df = events_df.join(users_df, on="user_id", how="left")
joined_df.write.format("delta").save("s3://lake/gold_events/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Filter / Salt NULL keys before Shuffle
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Strategy 1: If NULLs will NEVER match the dimension, split or pre-filter
valid_events = events_df.filter(F.col("user_id").isNotNull())
null_events = events_df.filter(F.col("user_id").isNull())

# Perform the join strictly on populated keys
joined_valid = valid_events.join(users_df, on="user_id", how="left")

# Union back with null events (adding NULL columns for users dimension)
for col_name in users_df.columns:
    if col_name != "user_id":
        null_events = null_events.withColumn(col_name, F.lit(None))

final_df = joined_valid.unionByName(null_events)

# Strategy 2: For Inner Joins, an explicit IS NOT NULL filter pushes down to scan:
# events_df.filter(F.col("user_id").isNotNull()).join(users_df, "user_id", "inner")
interview_takeaway: In any distributed join, NULL foreign keys provide zero join matches but hash to a single partition; always filter them before the shuffle or assign random negative surrogate IDs to distribute them evenly across reducers.

title: Default Placeholder Skew in GroupBy Aggregations
scenario: A retail analytics pipeline aggregates transaction volumes by store country. Upstream legacy point-of-sale systems populate `'UNKNOWN'` or `'N/A'` whenever GPS lookup fails. Out of 500 million transactions, 350 million contain `country = 'UNKNOWN'`. A simple `groupBy('country').agg(sum('amount'))` crashes with OutOfMemoryError.
symptom: Stage progress hangs at 99%. Spark UI Executor page shows one executor's heap memory climbing steadily to 100% until YARN/Kubernetes terminates the container with `Exit code 137 (OOMKilled)`.
root_cause: Tungsten uses an in-memory hash map (`BytesToBytesMap`) for aggregation. For the single key `'UNKNOWN'`, the hash map cannot be flushed efficiently, causing massive memory pressure and CPU thrashing during hash table resizing.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
tx_df = spark.read.parquet("s3://retail/transactions/")
# 350M rows out of 500M have country = 'UNKNOWN'
summary_df = tx_df.groupBy("country").agg(
    F.count("*").alias("tx_count"),
    F.sum("amount").alias("total_revenue")
)
summary_df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://retail/country_summary/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Two-Phase Aggregation with Key Salting on Placeholder
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Salt only the skewed key with 50 random buckets; leave normal keys untouched
salted_df = tx_df.withColumn(
    "salted_country",
    F.when(
        F.col("country") == "UNKNOWN",
        F.concat(F.col("country"), F.lit("_"), F.floor(F.rand() * 50))
    ).otherwise(F.col("country"))
)

# Phase 1: Partial Aggregation on Salted Key (distributes the 350M rows across 50 reducers)
partial_agg = salted_df.groupBy("salted_country").agg(
    F.count("*").alias("partial_count"),
    F.sum("amount").alias("partial_revenue")
)

# Phase 2: Strip Salt and Final Aggregation
final_summary = partial_agg.withColumn(
    "country",
    F.regexp_replace(F.col("salted_country"), "_[0-9]+$", "")
).groupBy("country").agg(
    F.sum("partial_count").alias("tx_count"),
    F.sum("partial_revenue").alias("total_revenue")
)
interview_takeaway: When high-cardinality placeholder values skew an aggregation, apply two-phase aggregation: salt the hot key with random integers, aggregate partially across reducers, strip the salt, and aggregate globally.

title: Asymmetric Dimension Join Skew Failing SortMergeJoin
scenario: A media streaming platform joins 1 billion stream events with an artists dimension table containing 2 million rows. Five pop megastars account for 40% of all streams. The query uses default `SortMergeJoin`. The shuffle stage spills 180 GB to disk, and the sort phase runs for 2 hours.
symptom: Spark UI shows `Shuffle Spill (Disk)` of 180 GB. Tasks handling megastar `artist_id` partitions spend 95% of execution time in `ExternalSorter.spill()`.
root_cause: SortMergeJoin forces both sides to shuffle and sort by join key. For hot keys, sorting 400 million rows in a single partition exceeds executor memory, spilling unsorted Tungsten pages to disk and thrashing I/O.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# artists_df is 250MB uncompressed (exceeds default autoBroadcastJoinThreshold of 10MB)
events_df = spark.read.table("lakehouse.streaming_events") # 1B rows
artists_df = spark.read.table("lakehouse.dim_artists")     # 2M rows (~250MB)

# Default SortMergeJoin triggered due to size > 10MB
result_df = events_df.join(artists_df, on="artist_id", how="inner")
result_df.write.format("delta").saveAsTable("lakehouse.fact_enriched_streams")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Force BroadcastHashJoin or Increase Broadcast Threshold
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Option A: Explicit Broadcast Hint (eliminates shuffle and sort entirely)
# Executor memory is 8GB+, so broadcasting 250MB is safe and optimal
result_df = events_df.join(F.broadcast(artists_df), on="artist_id", how="inner")

# Option B: Dynamically increase broadcast threshold in Spark session:
# spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", 500 * 1024 * 1024) # 500MB

# Option C: In Spark SQL:
# SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(a) */ * FROM streaming_events e JOIN dim_artists a ON e.artist_id = a.artist_id
interview_takeaway: Broadcast Hash Join completely avoids the shuffle and sort phases; whenever a skewed dimension table fits safely in driver and executor memory (up to a few GBs), broadcasting it bypasses data skew entirely.

title: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) Skew Join Threshold Tuning
scenario: A retail bank runs a daily reconciliation join between payments and ledger entries on Apache Spark 3.3. Despite `spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true`, one partition with a corporate clearinghouse ID runs 10x slower than all other partitions. AQE fails to split the skewed partition.
symptom: In the Spark UI SQL tab, the SortMergeJoin operator does not show `(skew=true)`, and no partition splitting sub-tasks are created.
root_cause: AQE skew join detection requires a partition to be both larger than `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` (default 256MB) AND larger than `skewedPartitionFactor` (default 5.0) times the median partition size. If median partitions are 60MB, a 280MB skewed partition is only 4.6x the median, failing the 5.0x factor rule.
failing_code:
# Failing Setup (Default Spark Conf):
# Median partition: 60MB. Skewed partition: 280MB (4.6x median, factor requires 5x)
# AQE treats this partition as normal, leaving 1 executor to process 280MB while others do 60MB.
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
# Default: spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor = 5.0
# Default: spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes = 256MB

ledger_df.join(payments_df, on="account_id").write.mode("overwrite").parquet("s3://bank/recon/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Lower AQE Skew Join Detection Thresholds
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")

# Lower the factor from 5.0 to 2.5 or 3.0 so moderate skews are intercepted
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor", "2.5")

# Lower threshold to 128MB or 64MB depending on executor core count
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes", "67108864") # 64MB

# Verify in execution plan: SortMergeJoin will now display SortMergeJoin(skew=true)
# and Spark will dynamically split the 280MB partition into 4-5 parallel reader tasks.
interview_takeaway: AQE skew join optimization uses dual criteria (absolute size and factor over median); in workloads with high-variance partitions, lower `skewedPartitionFactor` to 2.5-3.0 and `skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes` to 64MB so Spark automatically splits stragglers.

title: Two-Phase Key Salting for Massive Non-Broadcastable Joins
scenario: A telecom operator joins two 500GB tables: call data records (CDR) and cell tower telemetry. A primary antenna in Manhattan handles 15% of all calls (75GB). Both tables are too large to broadcast. AQE cannot completely balance the load because the skewed key exceeds memory limits. The join crashes with `FetchFailedException`.
symptom: Stage fails repeatedly with `FetchFailedException: Connection reset by peer` as executors hosting the Manhattan cell tower become unresponsive under memory pressure.
root_cause: When both sides of a skewed join are massive (hundreds of GBs), neither can be broadcast. Hash partitioning maps the hot key to a single reducer on both tables.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Neither table can be broadcast (both 500GB+)
cdrs = spark.read.table("lake.cdrs")       # tower_id 'T-NYC-001' has 150M rows
telemetry = spark.read.table("lake.telemetry") # tower_id 'T-NYC-001' has 80M rows

joined = cdrs.join(telemetry, on="tower_id", how="inner")
joined.write.format("delta").save("s3://lake/enriched_cdrs/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Isolated Salting of the Skewed Key
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

SALT_FACTOR = 32 # Spread hot key across 32 buckets

# 1. Salt the large skewed fact table with a random integer [0, SALT_FACTOR-1]
cdrs_salted = cdrs.withColumn(
    "salt",
    F.when(F.col("tower_id") == "T-NYC-001", F.floor(F.rand() * SALT_FACTOR)).otherwise(F.lit(0))
).withColumn("join_key", F.concat(F.col("tower_id"), F.lit("_"), F.col("salt")))

# 2. Replicate the dimension/telemetry records for the hot key across all salt values using explode
salt_array = F.array([F.lit(i) for i in range(SALT_FACTOR)])

telemetry_replicated = telemetry.withColumn(
    "salt",
    F.when(F.col("tower_id") == "T-NYC-001", F.explode(salt_array)).otherwise(F.lit(0))
).withColumn("join_key", F.concat(F.col("tower_id"), F.lit("_"), F.col("salt")))

# 3. Join on the salted composite key; drops hot-key partition size from 75GB to ~2.3GB!
joined_salted = cdrs_salted.join(telemetry_replicated, on="join_key", how="inner") \
    .drop("join_key", "salt")
interview_takeaway: When both sides of a join are too large to broadcast and have a known skewed key, salt the fact table with a random integer and explode the second table across all salt values to parallelize the join across $N$ partitions.

title: Explode-Induced Skew from Super-Entity Nested Arrays
scenario: A B2B SaaS platform processes company invoice documents. While 99% of companies have 10-50 line items per invoice, 3 global enterprise conglomerates have invoices containing 600,000 line items. Running `F.explode('line_items')` causes the executor handling those 3 records to crash with `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`.
symptom: Spark task begins normally, then CPU stalls and garbage collection time exceeds 85% of task run time before crashing with Heap OOM.
root_cause: `explode()` flattens arrays into individual rows within the same partition before writing. 600,000 complex struct objects instantiated in a single JVM thread create hundreds of millions of ephemeral Java objects, saturating Young and Old generation heap spaces.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
invoices_df = spark.read.json("s3://saas/invoices/") # 10M records
# Mega accounts have arrays with 600,000 line item structs
exploded_df = invoices_df.withColumn("item", F.explode("line_items")) \
    .select("company_id", "invoice_id", "item.item_id", "item.amount")

exploded_df.write.format("delta").save("s3://saas/line_items/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Split Mega-Arrays or Batch Using PySpark Higher-Order Functions
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Strategy 1: If calculating summaries (e.g. total amount), use higher-order functions WITHOUT exploding:
summary_df = invoices_df.withColumn(
    "total_invoice_amount",
    F.expr("aggregate(line_items, 0.0D, (acc, x) -> acc + x.amount)")
)

# Strategy 2: If explode is mandatory, repartition before explode on (company_id, invoice_id)
# or chunk mega arrays using slice() before exploding:
array_len = F.size("line_items")
chunked_df = invoices_df.withColumn(
    "chunks",
    F.when(array_len > 10000,
           F.transform(F.sequence(F.lit(1), array_len, F.lit(10000)),
                       lambda start: F.slice(F.col("line_items"), start, 10000)))
     .otherwise(F.array(F.col("line_items")))
).withColumn("chunk", F.explode("chunks")) \
 .withColumn("item", F.explode("chunk")) \
 .repartition(2000, "company_id")
interview_takeaway: Exploding multi-hundred-thousand element arrays creates JVM object allocation storms; replace naive `explode()` with higher-order functions (`aggregate`, `transform`) or chunk arrays into smaller batches before flattening.

title: Window Function Skew with Unbounded Preceding Windows
scenario: A fintech ledger calculates the cumulative running balance for all bank accounts using `SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY tx_timestamp ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)`. One central settlement account has 40 million transactions, while standard accounts have ~200. The stage running the window function spills 90 GB to disk and runs for 4 hours.
symptom: Spark UI shows 199 tasks completed in 2 minutes, while 1 task takes 4 hours, reading 40M rows in a single window frame with massive disk spill.
root_cause: A Window specification with `PARTITION BY account_id` forces all rows for a given account to be colocated on a single executor core in sorted order. Tungsten's `WindowExec` cannot distribute rows sharing the same partition key across multiple executors.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

tx_df = spark.read.table("lakehouse.bank_transactions")
window_spec = Window.partitionBy("account_id").orderBy("tx_timestamp") \
    .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)

running_df = tx_df.withColumn("running_balance", F.sum("amount").over(window_spec))
running_df.write.format("delta").saveAsTable("lakehouse.account_balances")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Day-Level Pre-Aggregation & Rollup Prefix Sum
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Step 1: Calculate daily balances per account (drastically reduces rows for settlement account)
daily_balances = tx_df.groupBy("account_id", F.to_date("tx_timestamp").alias("tx_date")) \
    .agg(F.sum("amount").alias("daily_total"))

# Step 2: Compute running balance of daily totals (compact data volume)
daily_window = Window.partitionBy("account_id").orderBy("tx_date") \
    .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)

daily_cumulative = daily_balances.withColumn("day_start_balance", F.sum("daily_total").over(daily_window) - F.col("daily_total"))

# Step 3: Compute intraday running balance partitioned by BOTH (account_id, tx_date)
intraday_window = Window.partitionBy("account_id", F.to_date("tx_timestamp")).orderBy("tx_timestamp") \
    .rowsBetween(Window.unboundedPreceding, Window.currentRow)

final_df = tx_df.withColumn("tx_date", F.to_date("tx_timestamp")) \
    .withColumn("intraday_running", F.sum("amount").over(intraday_window)) \
    .join(daily_cumulative.select("account_id", "tx_date", "day_start_balance"), on=["account_id", "tx_date"]) \
    .withColumn("running_balance", F.col("day_start_balance") + F.col("intraday_running"))
interview_takeaway: When window functions partition by a skewed key, you cannot partition across workers directly; break the problem into a two-level prefix sum: pre-aggregate into coarse time buckets (e.g. daily) and compute intraday windows partitioned by (account_id, date).

title: Uneven S3/ADLS Object Sizes & Non-Splittable Gzip Stragglers
scenario: A daily log ingestion job reads 5,000 files from cloud object storage. 4,999 files are 2MB each, but 1 file is an uncompressed or standard `.csv.gz` file of 42GB created by an upstream database dump. Reading the dataset generates 5,000 tasks, but task 5000 runs for 2.5 hours on a single executor while the cluster sits idle.
symptom: Spark cluster utilization drops to 2% (1 core active out of 100 cores), reading from a single massive `.csv.gz` object.
root_cause: Standard Gzip is non-splittable because it uses DEFLATE without sync markers. Spark cannot parallelize the read of a single `.gz` file across multiple tasks. Consequently, 1 core must sequentially decompress and parse all 42GB.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# The bucket contains 4,999 small files and one 42GB file: 'dump_full_raw.csv.gz'
df = spark.read.option("header", "true").csv("s3://raw-logs/2024-10-01/*.csv.gz")
df.write.format("delta").save("s3://bronze/logs/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Pre-split Non-Splittable Archives or Enforce Splittable Formats
# 1. Enforce splittable compression (bzip2, snappy, zstd) or Parquet upstream.
# 2. If stuck with existing monolithic .csv.gz, isolate the large file with a dedicated node
# or convert via shell streaming into chunked files:
# zcat dump_full_raw.csv.gz | split -l 1000000 - chunk_

# 3. For splittable files (uncompressed, Parquet, Bzip2), tune maxPartitionBytes:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes", "134217728") # 128MB per partition
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.openCostInBytes", "4194304")      # 4MB packing cost

# Read splittable files: Spark will automatically carve 42GB into ~336 parallel tasks
df_splittable = spark.read.parquet("s3://raw-logs/2024-10-01/*.parquet")
interview_takeaway: Standard Gzip (`.gz`) is fundamentally non-splittable in Hadoop/Spark; single giant gzip files bottleneck execution to a single core regardless of cluster size. Require splittable codecs (Bzip2, Snappy, Zstandard) or Parquet/ORC at ingestion boundaries.

title: Stateful Structured Streaming Session Skew Ballooning State Store
scenario: A cybersecurity lakehouse processes IoT events using `flatMapGroupsWithState` to detect anomalous device sessions. A compromised router infected with malware emits 20,000 heartbeat packets per second, while regular devices emit 1 every 5 minutes. Within 4 hours, the streaming query latency spikes from 3 seconds to 12 minutes, and the executor hosting the malware state crashes with `StateStoreProvider OOM`.
symptom: Streaming query micro-batch processing time climbs continuously. Spark UI Structured Streaming tab shows watermark progressing but state store memory on one executor growing to 15GB+.
root_cause: The default HDFS/Memory StateStore keeps state in JVM heap. The hot key accumulates hundreds of thousands of state transitions in memory. Furthermore, hash partitioning sends all updates for that compromised device to one executor state partition.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Default in-memory state store
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
               "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.HDFSBackedStateStoreProvider")

stream_df = spark.readStream.format("kafka").load() \
    .selectExpr("CAST(key AS STRING) as device_id", "CAST(value AS STRING) as payload", "timestamp")

# Stateful mapping without state limits
def update_session(key, values, state):
    current = state.getOption() or []
    for v in values:
        current.append(v) # Unbounded accumulation for infected router
    state.update(current)
    return [Row(device_id=key, event_count=len(current))]
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: RocksDB Off-Heap StateStore + Event Throttling & Watermarking
# 1. Switch to RocksDB State Store (stores state off-heap on local SSDs, preventing JVM heap OOM)
spark.conf.set(
    "spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass",
    "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider"
)

# 2. Implement strict TTL and bounded state history in state function
from pyspark.sql.streaming import GroupStateTimeout

def update_session_bounded(key, values, state):
    if state.hasTimedOut:
        state.remove()
        return []
    
    current_count = state.getOption() or 0
    new_events = list(values)
    
    # Cap maximum accumulated state to prevent bot poison pills
    if current_count > 10000:
        # Flag alert and evict or drop
        state.setTimeoutDuration("1 hour")
        return [Row(device_id=key, status="ABUSE_THROTTLED")]
        
    state.update(current_count + len(new_events))
    state.setTimeoutDuration("30 minutes")
    return [Row(device_id=key, status="OK")]
interview_takeaway: For stateful Spark streaming on skewed real-time streams, always switch from the default in-memory HDFS state store to the off-heap RocksDB state store and enforce strict per-key state bounding and timeouts.

title: Skewed Ingestion in Delta Lake: Directory Partitioning vs Liquid Clustering
scenario: An ad-tech platform stores 50TB of clickstream data partitioned physically by `PARTITIONED BY (advertiser_id, date)`. Top advertisers (Google, Amazon) have billions of clicks generating 100,000 files per date folder, while long-tail advertisers generate 1KB files. Query performance collapses due to the small file problem for small advertisers and massive file scanning for large advertisers.
symptom: Metadata queries against the Delta transaction log take 4 minutes just to list partitions (`AnalysisException: Path does not exist / slow metastore`). Queries on small advertisers spend 99% of time in file open overhead.
root_cause: Hive-style directory partitioning on high-cardinality or skewed columns creates rigid directory trees. It leads to the 'small files problem' for low-volume keys and 'giant skewed partitions' for high-volume keys.
failing_code:
-- Failing Delta DDL:
CREATE TABLE clickstream_events (
    click_id STRING,
    advertiser_id STRING,
    event_timestamp TIMESTAMP,
    bid_amount DECIMAL(10,2)
) USING DELTA
PARTITIONED BY (advertiser_id, date(event_timestamp));
-- Results in 500,000 directory paths in cloud storage!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Delta Lake 3.x Liquid Clustering
-- Liquid clustering avoids physical folder partitioning entirely.
-- It dynamically clusters data using Hilbert curves without partition rigidity.

CREATE TABLE clickstream_events (
    click_id STRING,
    advertiser_id STRING,
    event_timestamp TIMESTAMP,
    bid_amount DECIMAL(10,2)
) USING DELTA
CLUSTER BY (advertiser_id, event_timestamp);

-- Regular automated or scheduled maintenance:
OPTIMIZE clickstream_events;
-- Liquid clustering automatically balances skewed advertiser data across uniform 128MB-1GB files
-- and rewrites only the necessary cluster boundaries without locking entire partition trees.
interview_takeaway: Never physically partition Delta tables by high-cardinality or skewed columns; adopt Delta Lake Liquid Clustering (`CLUSTER BY`), which dynamically groups data without directory proliferation and adapts to skew.

title: NOT IN Subquery Returning Zero Rows Due to a Single NULL
scenario: A compliance reporting pipeline extracts active customers who have not received marketing opt-out notices. The query uses `WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM opt_out_notices)`. Although there are 5 million active customers and only 2,000 opt-outs, the query returns zero rows in production.
symptom: Query returns an empty result set (0 records) without throwing any syntax or runtime errors.
root_cause: Under ANSI three-valued logic (3VL), if the subquery returns even a single row with `customer_id IS NULL`, `x NOT IN (val1, val2, NULL)` evaluates to `UNKNOWN` (equivalent to FALSE). Because `x = NULL` is UNKNOWN, `NOT (UNKNOWN)` remains UNKNOWN, discarding every single record.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
-- If opt_out_notices contains even 1 row where customer_id IS NULL, entire query returns 0 rows!
SELECT *
FROM customers
WHERE customer_id NOT IN (
    SELECT customer_id FROM opt_out_notices
);
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Use NOT EXISTS or LEFT ANTI JOIN
-- Option A: NOT EXISTS (Null-Safe)
SELECT c.*
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM opt_out_notices o
    WHERE c.customer_id = o.customer_id
);

-- Option B: PySpark Left Anti Join (Optimized Catalyst Plan)
# df_customers.join(df_opt_outs, on="customer_id", how="left_anti")

-- Option C: If NOT IN is mandatory, explicitly filter NULLs in subquery:
-- WHERE customer_id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM opt_out_notices WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL)
interview_takeaway: `NOT IN` with a nullable subquery is an infamous SQL trap: a single NULL collapses the entire predicate to UNKNOWN; always use `LEFT ANTI JOIN` or `NOT EXISTS` in production Spark pipelines.

title: COUNT(column) vs COUNT(*) vs COUNT(1) Metric Inaccuracies
scenario: A financial KPI dashboard reports that total transactions dropped by 40% month-over-month. Upon investigation, total transactions did not drop; rather, a new mobile app release temporarily stopped sending optional `session_id` tags, and the pipeline calculated transaction count as `COUNT(session_id)`.
symptom: Executive metrics show phantom drops in business volume without any system outages or error alerts.
root_cause: `COUNT(column_name)` counts only non-null values for that specific column. `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(1)` count all rows in the group regardless of nullability.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
tx_df = spark.read.table("lakehouse.transactions")

# session_id was made optional, introducing 40% NULLs
daily_metrics = tx_df.groupBy("tx_date").agg(
    F.count("session_id").alias("total_transactions"), # SILENT METRIC CORRUPTION
    F.sum("amount").alias("gross_revenue")
)
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Explicit COUNT(*) or COUNT(1) for Total Row Volume
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

daily_metrics = tx_df.groupBy("tx_date").agg(
    F.count(F.lit(1)).alias("total_transactions"), # Correctly counts all rows
    F.count("session_id").alias("sessions_with_id"),
    F.sum("amount").alias("gross_revenue")
)

# In Spark SQL:
# SELECT tx_date, COUNT(*) AS total_tx, COUNT(session_id) AS valid_sessions FROM transactions GROUP BY tx_date
interview_takeaway: `COUNT(column)` ignores NULL values while `COUNT(*)` counts physical records; never use `COUNT(column)` for business volume metrics unless deliberately filtering missing values.

title: Equality Comparison with NULL: col = NULL vs eqNullSafe (<=>)
scenario: A data quality reconciliation job checks whether records in staging match records in gold. When matching nullable discount codes (`discount_code = 'NONE'` or `NULL`), matching rows with `NULL` on both sides are dropped. The reconciliation flags 250,000 false-positive discrepancies.
symptom: Records with NULL on both source and target fail join or filter conditions and are reported as non-matching.
root_cause: In standard SQL, `NULL = NULL` is NOT TRUE; it evaluates to `NULL` (UNKNOWN). Therefore, `staging.discount_code = gold.discount_code` evaluates to NULL, dropping rows from INNER JOIN or equality checks.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Comparing two DataFrames with nullable columns
mismatches = staging_df.join(gold_df, on="record_id") \
    .filter(staging_df["discount_code"] != gold_df["discount_code"])
# Rows where both are NULL are excluded from the comparison, silently hiding or creating discrepancies!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Use eqNullSafe (<=>) Operator
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# eqNullSafe (<=>) evaluates NULL <=> NULL as TRUE, and NULL <=> 'VALUE' as FALSE
mismatches = staging_df.join(gold_df, on="record_id") \
    .filter(~(staging_df["discount_code"].eqNullSafe(gold_df["discount_code"])))

# In Spark SQL:
# SELECT * FROM staging s JOIN gold g ON s.record_id = g.record_id
# WHERE NOT (s.discount_code <=> g.discount_code)
interview_takeaway: In SQL and Spark, `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN; always use the null-safe equality operator `<=>` (`eqNullSafe` in PySpark) when comparing nullable attributes or joining on nullable dimensions.

title: Silent NULL Infiltration in String Concatenation
scenario: A customer profile service concatenates name fields: `title`, `first_name`, `middle_name`, and `last_name` to create a `full_name` column. Customers with no middle name (60% of the customer base) end up with `full_name = NULL`.
symptom: Customer identity directory displays NULL for majority of user names, leading to critical downstream export failures.
root_cause: The SQL standard `CONCAT(a, b, c)` function returns `NULL` if any individual argument is `NULL`.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
users = spark.read.table("lakehouse.dim_users")
# If middle_name is NULL, entire full_name becomes NULL!
users_with_name = users.withColumn(
    "full_name",
    F.concat(F.col("first_name"), F.lit(" "), F.col("middle_name"), F.lit(" "), F.col("last_name"))
)
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Use concat_ws() or coalesce()
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# concat_ws (Concatenate With Separator) automatically ignores NULL values!
users_with_name = users.withColumn(
    "full_name",
    F.concat_ws(" ", F.col("first_name"), F.col("middle_name"), F.col("last_name"))
)

# In Spark SQL:
# SELECT concat_ws(' ', first_name, middle_name, last_name) AS full_name FROM dim_users;
interview_takeaway: `concat()` is poisoned by a single NULL operand; always use `concat_ws()` (concatenate with separator), which inherently skips NULL values and prevents silent data nullification.

title: Outer Join Predicate Placement Turning Outer Joins into Inner Joins
scenario: An audit query needs all registered suppliers, along with their active purchase orders if any exist. The developer writes a `LEFT OUTER JOIN` between suppliers and purchase orders, but adds `WHERE po.order_status = 'ACTIVE'`. As a result, all 10,000 suppliers with zero purchase orders are eliminated from the report.
symptom: Suppliers with no purchase orders are missing; query returns only suppliers who currently have active orders.
root_cause: The `WHERE` clause is evaluated after the `LEFT JOIN`. For suppliers with no purchase orders, `po.order_status` is `NULL`. The predicate `WHERE NULL = 'ACTIVE'` evaluates to FALSE, discarding all unmatched left-table rows and mutating the LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
SELECT s.supplier_id, s.supplier_name, po.order_id, po.amount
FROM suppliers s
LEFT JOIN purchase_orders po ON s.supplier_id = po.supplier_id
WHERE po.order_status = 'ACTIVE'; -- Kills the LEFT JOIN!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Move Filter Predicate into ON Join Condition
SELECT s.supplier_id, s.supplier_name, po.order_id, po.amount
FROM suppliers s
LEFT JOIN purchase_orders po 
    ON s.supplier_id = po.supplier_id 
    AND po.order_status = 'ACTIVE'; -- Filters right table BEFORE the join!

-- In PySpark:
# suppliers_df.join(
#     po_df.filter(F.col("order_status") == "ACTIVE"),
#     on="supplier_id",
#     how="left"
# )
interview_takeaway: Filtering right-table columns in the `WHERE` clause eliminates rows with generated NULLs, turning a LEFT OUTER JOIN into an INNER JOIN; always push right-side predicates into the `ON` clause or pre-filter the right DataFrame.

title: PySpark Namespace Collision: F.coalesce() vs DataFrame.coalesce()
scenario: A data engineer attempting to replace null phone numbers with secondary phone numbers writes: `df.withColumn('phone', coalesce('primary_phone', 'secondary_phone'))`. However, because they did `from pyspark.sql.functions import *` and had existing DataFrame references, the pipeline throws `AttributeError` or runs partition reduction unexpectedly.
symptom: `TypeError: Invalid argument, not a string or column` or unexpected shuffle behavior.
root_cause: `DataFrame.coalesce(numPartitions)` reduces the number of partitions without shuffling. `pyspark.sql.functions.coalesce(*cols)` returns the first non-null column. In wildcard imports or careless aliasing, namespace collisions create obscure runtime errors.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
from pyspark.sql import *
from pyspark.sql.functions import *

# Ambiguous function resolution / anti-pattern wildcard import
# If coalesce is overwritten or called on wrong object:
df = spark.read.table("contacts")
df = df.withColumn("phone", coalesce("mobile", "home", "office"))
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Strict Namespace Aliasing
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.read.table("contacts")

# F.coalesce strictly references the column-level null-replacement expression
df = df.withColumn(
    "phone",
    F.coalesce(F.col("mobile"), F.col("home"), F.col("office"), F.lit("NO_PHONE"))
)

# DataFrame.coalesce is used strictly for partition reduction:
# df = df.coalesce(4)
interview_takeaway: Never use wildcard imports (`from pyspark.sql.functions import *`); always import `from pyspark.sql import functions as F` to prevent namespace collisions between `F.coalesce()` (null replacement) and `DataFrame.coalesce()` (partition reduction).

title: Window Frame Specification NULL Ordering in LAG and LEAD
scenario: A crypto exchange calculates the price delta between consecutive trades using `LAG(price) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY trade_timestamp)`. Due to an upstream sensor bug, 1% of trades have `trade_timestamp IS NULL`. In Spark SQL, the default ordering places NULLs first, resulting in distorted price deltas for the earliest legitimate trades.
symptom: The first legitimate trade of the day compares its price against a null timestamp trade, resulting in wrong deltas.
root_cause: In Spark SQL, default ascending order treats NULLs as the lowest value (`ASC NULLS FIRST`). If timestamps contain NULLs, they cluster at the start of the window frame, displacing the true earliest trades.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

trades = spark.read.table("lake.trades")
# Default orderBy places NULL timestamps first!
w = Window.partitionBy("symbol").orderBy("trade_timestamp")

trades_with_delta = trades.withColumn("prev_price", F.lag("price", 1).over(w)) \
    .withColumn("price_delta", F.col("price") - F.col("prev_price"))
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Explicit Null Ordering & Pre-Filtering
from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Step 1: Filter out or isolate corrupt trades with NULL timestamps
clean_trades = trades.filter(F.col("trade_timestamp").isNotNull())

# Step 2: Enforce explicit NULL ordering in Window definition
w = Window.partitionBy("symbol").orderBy(F.col("trade_timestamp").asc_nulls_last())

trades_with_delta = clean_trades.withColumn("prev_price", F.lag("price", 1).over(w)) \
    .withColumn("price_delta", F.col("price") - F.col("prev_price"))

# In Spark SQL:
# LAG(price) OVER (PARTITION BY symbol ORDER BY trade_timestamp ASC NULLS LAST)
interview_takeaway: Spark's default sort behavior is `ASC NULLS FIRST`; in time-series window functions (`LAG`, `LEAD`), always specify `asc_nulls_last()` or filter NULL timestamps upstream to avoid window boundary poisoning.

title: Null Key Shuffling to a Single Reducer during repartition(col)
scenario: A data engineer wants to prepare a 1TB dataset for high-speed downstream filtering by running `df.repartition(200, 'region_code')`. Because 25% of legacy records have `region_code IS NULL`, the repartitioning job creates 199 partitions of ~3.7GB and 1 partition of 250GB, causing severe out-of-memory errors in downstream stages.
symptom: Downstream jobs fail with `FetchFailedException` or `GC overhead limit exceeded` when reading the single 250GB partition.
root_cause: Hash partitioning computes hash codes using `Murmur3Hash`. All NULL values yield a hash of 0 (or a fixed bucket), sending all 250GB of NULL records into a single physical partition.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/raw_transactions/")
# 25% of rows have region_code = NULL
repartitioned_df = df.repartition(200, "region_code")
repartitioned_df.write.format("parquet").save("s3://lake/partitioned_tx/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Salt NULLs Before Repartitioning
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Assign random synthetic keys to NULLs so they scatter across all 200 partitions
salted_df = df.withColumn(
    "repart_key",
    F.when(F.col("region_code").isNull(), F.concat(F.lit("NULL_"), F.floor(F.rand() * 200)))
     .otherwise(F.col("region_code"))
)

repartitioned_df = salted_df.repartition(200, "repart_key").drop("repart_key")
repartitioned_df.write.format("parquet").save("s3://lake/partitioned_tx/")
interview_takeaway: `df.repartition(N, 'col')` routes all NULL values to a single partition; when partitioning on a nullable column with high nullity, salt the NULL values with random integers to distribute them evenly across physical partitions.

title: Three-Valued Logic in CASE WHEN Expressions Without ELSE Default
scenario: A medical risk model categorizes patient blood pressure using a `CASE WHEN` statement: `CASE WHEN bp < 120 THEN 'NORMAL' WHEN bp >= 120 THEN 'ELEVATED' END`. Upstream sensor telemetry frequently sends `bp = NULL`. Because there is no `ELSE` branch, these records become `NULL`, breaking downstream mandatory categorical encoders.
symptom: Downstream ML feature pipeline crashes with `IllegalArgumentException: Field status contains unexpected null values`.
root_cause: If no `WHEN` clause evaluates to TRUE and no `ELSE` clause is specified, SQL `CASE WHEN` defaults to `NULL`. With three-valued logic, `NULL < 120` is UNKNOWN and `NULL >= 120` is UNKNOWN, falling through to the omitted ELSE.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
SELECT patient_id,
       CASE 
           WHEN systolic < 120 THEN 'NORMAL'
           WHEN systolic >= 120 AND systolic < 140 THEN 'ELEVATED'
           WHEN systolic >= 140 THEN 'HIGH'
       END AS bp_category -- Missing ELSE! If systolic is NULL, returns NULL
FROM vitals_stream;
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Explicit Null Check and Fallback ELSE Clause
SELECT patient_id,
       CASE 
           WHEN systolic IS NULL THEN 'UNKNOWN_MISSING'
           WHEN systolic < 120 THEN 'NORMAL'
           WHEN systolic < 140 THEN 'ELEVATED'
           ELSE 'HIGH'
       END AS bp_category
FROM vitals_stream;

-- In PySpark:
# F.when(F.col("systolic").isNull(), "UNKNOWN_MISSING") \
#  .when(F.col("systolic") < 120, "NORMAL") \
#  .when(F.col("systolic") < 140, "ELEVATED") \
#  .otherwise("HIGH")
interview_takeaway: In SQL `CASE WHEN` constructs, omitted `ELSE` clauses silently evaluate to `NULL`; in production pipelines, always provide an explicit `otherwise()`/`ELSE` clause and handle NULL input states explicitly.

title: Enforcing Non-Null Constraints in Delta Lake & Handling Ingestion Violations
scenario: An enterprise lakehouse serves a gold dimensional table `dim_customers`. Business requirements mandate that `customer_id` and `tax_id` must never be NULL. However, periodic ingestion batches containing corrupted NULL tax IDs cause the entire pipeline write to fail midway, leaving the orchestration DAG in a failed state.
symptom: `DeltaInvariantViolationException: CHECK constraint check_tax_id (tax_id IS NOT NULL) violated by row with tax_id: null`.
root_cause: Delta Lake CHECK constraints and NOT NULL invariants abort the entire transaction when a single violating row is encountered to preserve ACID guarantees.
failing_code:
-- Failing Setup:
ALTER TABLE gold.dim_customers ADD CONSTRAINT check_tax_id CHECK (tax_id IS NOT NULL);

-- Later, an ingestion batch with 1 NULL tax_id out of 10 million rows fails the entire job:
-- df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("gold.dim_customers")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Zero-Loss Quarantine Split Before Gold Append
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

incoming_df = spark.read.table("silver.customers_staging")

# Split incoming batch into Valid Records and Quarantine Records
valid_records = incoming_df.filter(F.col("customer_id").isNotNull() & F.col("tax_id").isNotNull())
quarantined_records = incoming_df.filter(F.col("customer_id").isNull() | F.col("tax_id").isNull()) \
    .withColumn("quarantine_reason", F.lit("VIOLATION: tax_id or customer_id IS NULL")) \
    .withColumn("quarantine_timestamp", F.current_timestamp())

# 1. Append valid records safely to Gold (guaranteed to satisfy constraints)
valid_records.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("gold.dim_customers")

# 2. Divert corrupt records to Dead-Letter Quarantine table for automated alerting
quarantined_records.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("audit.quarantined_customers")
interview_takeaway: Delta Lake constraints strictly enforce ACID integrity by throwing invariant exceptions on violation; protect production pipelines by implementing a pre-write split pattern that diverts violating rows to a quarantine table while committing valid records.

title: Parquet Column Case Sensitivity and spark.sql.caseSensitive Collisions
scenario: A legacy ingestion pipeline creates Parquet files where some files have column `CustomerId` while other files created by another service have `customerid`. When reading the combined directory with Spark's default configuration, queries either fail or produce inconsistent results.
symptom: `AnalysisException: Found duplicate column(s) in the table schema: customerid` or silent column nullification.
root_cause: By default, Spark SQL is case-insensitive (`spark.sql.caseSensitive = false`), but Parquet file metadata is strictly case-sensitive. When schema inference encounters both `CustomerId` and `customerid`, Catalyst treats them as duplicates or fails during partition resolution.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Directory contains files with both 'CustomerId' and 'customerid'
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://lake/legacy_customers/")
# Throws AnalysisException: Reference 'customerid' is ambiguous or duplicate
interview_takeaway: Spark SQL is case-insensitive by default while storage formats like Parquet are case-sensitive; enforce lowercase snake_case schema normalization at the raw ingestion layer to prevent ambiguous reference exceptions.

title: Missing Columns in Historical Parquet Partitions during Schema Evolution
scenario: A data warehouse reads a partitioned Parquet table spanning 3 years. On October 1st, upstream added a new column `loyalty_tier`. When downstream analytical queries select `loyalty_tier` across the entire 3-year date range, Spark throws `AnalysisException: cannot resolve 'loyalty_tier'` because schema inference only inspected older partitions.
symptom: `AnalysisException: cannot resolve 'loyalty_tier' given input columns: [...]` when reading partitioned Parquet directories.
root_cause: To avoid slow cloud storage metadata scans, Spark's Parquet reader only infers schema from a subset of files (or summary metadata files). If older files lack the new column and summary metadata is absent, Spark assumes the column does not exist across the dataset.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Older partitions (2021-2023) lack loyalty_tier; 2024 partitions contain it
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://warehouse/fact_sales/")
df.select("customer_id", "loyalty_tier").show()
# Fails with AnalysisException: cannot resolve loyalty_tier
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Enable mergeSchema or Migrate to Delta Lake
# Option 1: Enable mergeSchema option during Parquet read
df = spark.read.option("mergeSchema", "true").parquet("s3://warehouse/fact_sales/")
df.select("customer_id", "loyalty_tier").show()
# Older partitions will automatically output NULL for loyalty_tier

# Option 2: (Best Practice) Convert legacy Parquet to Delta Lake:
# Delta maintains an explicit ACID transaction log that tracks schema evolution globally:
# CONVERT TO DELTA parquet.`s3://warehouse/fact_sales/`;
interview_takeaway: Reading evolved Parquet partitions requires `.option('mergeSchema', 'true')` to merge schemas across historical files; adopting Delta Lake eliminates this overhead by maintaining the canonical schema in its ACID transaction log.

title: JSON Payload Field Polymorphism (Primitive String vs JSON Object)
scenario: A telemetry pipeline ingests mobile device logs from IoT devices. In firmware v1, the `metadata` field was serialized as a plain string: `"metadata": "offline_mode"`. In firmware v2, it was upgraded to a nested object: `"metadata": {"network": "5G", "battery": 92}`. Spark's JSON reader crashes with a schema parsing mismatch.
symptom: `SparkException: Malformed records are detected in record parsing` or `metadata` column becomes NULL for entire batches.
root_cause: Spark's DataFrame schema is strictly typed. A column cannot simultaneously be of type `StringType` and `StructType`. Schema inference either picks StructType (causing string payloads to be marked malformed) or StringType (failing nested queries).
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Batch contains both: {"metadata": "v1_plain"} and {"metadata": {"network": "5G"}}
schema = "device_id STRING, metadata STRUCT<network: STRING, battery: INT>"
df = spark.read.schema(schema).json("s3://iot/telemetry/")
df.show() # Rows with string metadata become NULL and land in _corrupt_record!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Read Field as Raw String and Parse Conditionally
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType

# Step 1: Read the polymorphic field generically as raw STRING
raw_schema = "device_id STRING, metadata STRING"
df = spark.read.schema(raw_schema).json("s3://iot/telemetry/")

# Step 2: Define struct schema for complex variant
meta_struct_schema = StructType([
    StructField("network", StringType(), True),
    StructField("battery", IntegerType(), True)
])

# Step 3: Parse conditionally using from_json and regex detection
processed_df = df.withColumn(
    "is_json_object", F.col("metadata").startswith("{")
).withColumn(
    "parsed_metadata",
    F.when(F.col("is_json_object"), F.from_json(F.col("metadata"), meta_struct_schema))
     .otherwise(F.lit(None))
).withColumn(
    "legacy_metadata_str",
    F.when(~F.col("is_json_object"), F.col("metadata")).otherwise(F.lit(None))
)
interview_takeaway: When upstream schemas exhibit polymorphic fields (e.g. primitive vs struct), read the column as raw `StringType` and use `from_json()` inside conditional `F.when()` expressions to deserialize valid JSON objects without dropping legacy strings.

title: Delta Lake mergeSchema vs overwriteSchema Dynamics
scenario: A daily ETL job reloads an aggregated gold table with `mode('overwrite')`. One day, upstream changes a column name from `total_rev` to `revenue`. The engineer uses `.option('mergeSchema', 'true')` with overwrite. Unexpectedly, the resulting Delta table now has BOTH `total_rev` (all NULLs for today) and `revenue`, permanently bloating the table schema.
symptom: The table schema grows monotonically with dead legacy columns; queries selecting old column names return NULL instead of failing.
root_cause: `.option('mergeSchema', 'true')` with `mode('overwrite')` merges the incoming schema with the existing historical schema; it does NOT delete missing columns. To completely replace the schema, `overwriteSchema` is required.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Desired behavior: Replace table schema completely with incoming DataFrame schema
df_today = spark.read.table("silver.daily_sales") # has new column 'revenue' instead of 'total_rev'

df_today.write.format("delta") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .option("mergeSchema", "true") \ # TRAP: Keeps total_rev in schema forever!
    .saveAsTable("gold.fact_sales")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Use overwriteSchema for Intentional Full Redefinition
# When intentionally redefining the schema during a table overwrite:
df_today.write.format("delta") \
    .mode("overwrite") \
    .option("overwriteSchema", "true") \ # Cleanly replaces table schema
    .saveAsTable("gold.fact_sales")

# Use mergeSchema strictly for append operations where new optional columns are added:
# df_incoming.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("gold.fact_sales")
interview_takeaway: In Delta Lake, `.option('mergeSchema', 'true')` unions the schemas and preserves legacy columns; use `.option('overwriteSchema', 'true')` with `mode('overwrite')` to intentionally drop old columns and reset the table schema definition.

title: Data Type Widening Failures in Parquet Dictionary Encoding
scenario: A financial transaction ID column exceeds $2^{31}-1$ (2.14 billion), requiring a type migration from `IntegerType` (INT) to `LongType` (BIGINT). Upstream starts writing INT64 Parquet files. When Spark reads historical INT32 Parquet files alongside new INT64 files, the job crashes with `ParquetDecodingException`.
symptom: `org.apache.parquet.io.ParquetDecodingException: Can not read value at 0 in block 0 in file ... INT32 is not compatible with INT64`.
root_cause: Parquet physical encoding stores primitive types at the page level. Reading physical INT32 data as INT64 requires vectorization support or explicit widening. In older Spark runtimes, vectorized Parquet readers fail to promote physical INT32 to logical INT64 on the fly.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Table contains a mix of older INT32 Parquet files and new INT64 files
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.enableVectorizedReader", "true")

df = spark.read.schema("tx_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE").parquet("s3://lake/transactions/")
df.count() # Crashes with ParquetDecodingException: INT32 not compatible with INT64
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Enable Type Widening or Fall Back Vectorized Reader
# Option 1: In Delta Lake 3.2+ / Databricks Runtime 13+, enable automatic Type Widening:
# ALTER TABLE transactions SET TBLPROPERTIES('delta.enableTypeWidening' = 'true');
# ALTER TABLE transactions CHANGE COLUMN tx_id TYPE BIGINT;

# Option 2: For standard Parquet, disable vectorized reader for the schema transition job:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.enableVectorizedReader", "false")
# Non-vectorized reader safely promotes INT32 to INT64 in JVM memory

# Option 3: Standardize by rewriting historical partitions:
# spark.read.schema("tx_id INT, amount DOUBLE").parquet("s3://old/").withColumn("tx_id", F.col("tx_id").cast("BIGINT")).write...
interview_takeaway: Vectorized Parquet readers reject physical type mismatches (INT32 vs INT64); resolve this by enabling Delta Lake Type Widening or temporarily disabling `spark.sql.parquet.enableVectorizedReader` during migration pipelines.

title: Auto Loader schemaEvolutionMode rescue and _rescued_data Column Triage
scenario: A cloud ingestion pipeline uses Databricks Auto Loader (`cloudFiles`) to ingest telemetry JSON files. An upstream team unexpectedly changes `user_id` from integer `12345` to UUID string `'usr_98124a'`. With schema evolution set to rescue, the pipeline doesn't fail, but analytical queries suddenly report that 100% of new users have `user_id = NULL`.
symptom: No pipeline failure occurs, but critical business columns turn NULL silently, and the hidden column `_rescued_data` inflates in size.
root_cause: When `cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode = 'rescue'` is used, any incoming data that does not match the inferred or declared schema (e.g. string value for an integer column) is diverted into the `_rescued_data` JSON column to prevent ingestion failure.
failing_code:
# Failing Ingestion Pattern:
stream_df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") \
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") \
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "s3://lake/checkpoints/schema/") \
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "rescue") \ # Silently rescues mismatches
    .load("s3://lake/raw_landing/")

# Downstream ignores _rescued_data:
stream_df.writeStream.format("delta").table("bronze.telemetry")
# user_id is typed as INT; string UUIDs become NULL in user_id and are rescued!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Active Rescued Data Monitoring and Type Evolution
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# 1. Configure Auto Loader with addNewColumns to allow safe widening:
stream_df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") \
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") \
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "s3://lake/checkpoints/schema/") \
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "addNewColumns") \
    .load("s3://lake/raw_landing/")

# 2. Add an automated Data Quality alert check on _rescued_data:
def alert_on_rescued_data(batch_df, batch_id):
    rescued_count = batch_df.filter(F.col("_rescued_data").isNotNull()).count()
    if rescued_count > 0:
        # Trigger automated PagerDuty / Slack webhook alert:
        print(f"WARNING: Batch {batch_id} contained {rescued_count} rescued records due to schema drift!")
    batch_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("bronze.telemetry")
interview_takeaway: Auto Loader's `rescue` mode prevents pipeline downtime by diverting type mismatches to `_rescued_data`; always implement monitoring on `_rescued_data` to detect silent column nullification caused by breaking upstream type changes.

title: Struct Field Reordering in Parquet Causing Misaligned Column Values
scenario: A healthcare system stores patient address as a struct: `STRUCT<street: STRING, city: STRING>`. An external microservice writes Parquet files where the struct fields are ordered `STRUCT<city: STRING, street: STRING>`. When Spark reads the combined dataset, patient street addresses appear in the `city` column and city names appear in the `street` column.
symptom: Values are silently swapped between adjacent struct fields without any error or warning.
root_cause: Legacy Parquet readers resolve struct fields positionally (by ordinal index) rather than by name. If two fields share the same datatype (`StringType`), Spark maps physical field 0 to logical field 0 regardless of field names.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Setup:
# File A written with: struct<street: "123 Main St", city: "Seattle">
# File B written with: struct<city: "Austin", street: "456 Oak Ave">

# Default Spark Parquet Reader without by-name resolution:
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://health/patients/")
df.select("address.city", "address.street").show()
# File B displays: city = "456 Oak Ave", street = "Austin"! SILENT CORRUPTION!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Enable Name-Based Struct Resolution or Column Mapping
# Option 1: Tell Spark to resolve Parquet fields by Name rather than Position:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.fieldId.enabled", "true")

# Option 2: In Delta Lake, enable Column Mapping by Name:
# ALTER TABLE patients SET TBLPROPERTIES (
#   'delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name',
#   'delta.minReaderVersion' = '2',
#   'delta.minWriterVersion' = '5'
# );
# Delta column mapping guarantees that fields are strictly mapped by metadata UUID/name,
# completely preventing physical ordinal alignment corruption.
interview_takeaway: Positional schema resolution in Parquet silently swaps data between struct fields of identical types; eliminate positional ambiguity by enabling Delta Lake Column Mapping (`delta.columnMapping.mode = 'name'`).

title: Schema Evolution during Streaming MERGE INTO Delta Tables
scenario: A CDC stream merges real-time database updates into a Delta silver table using `foreachBatch` and `MERGE INTO`. When the source database adds a new column `middle_name`, the streaming micro-batch fails with `AnalysisException: Cannot resolve [middle_name] in target table`.
symptom: Streaming pipeline crashes on micro-batch execution; retries fail repeatedly, halting real-time ingestion.
root_cause: Delta Lake `MERGE INTO` does not automatically evolve the target table schema by default unless explicit Spark configuration flags or merge clauses permit schema evolution.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Streaming foreachBatch:
def upsert_to_delta(microBatchDF, batchId):
    # Fails when microBatchDF contains new column not yet present in target Delta table
    microBatchDF.createOrReplaceTempView("updates")
    microBatchDF._jdf.sparkSession().sql("""
        MERGE INTO silver_table t
        USING updates s
        ON t.id = s.id
        WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
        WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
    """)

streaming_df.writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert_to_delta).start()
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Enable Schema Evolution on Delta Merge
# Enable automatic schema evolution for Delta MERGE operations in Spark session:
spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled", "true")

# Alternative: In standard Delta Lake (Open Source), use the Python DeltaTable API:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable

def upsert_to_delta_with_evolution(microBatchDF, batchId):
    deltaTable = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "silver_table")
    
    # spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled", "true")
    # allows Delta to automatically ALTER the target table to add incoming columns:
    (deltaTable.alias("t")
     .merge(microBatchDF.alias("s"), "t.id = s.id")
     .whenMatchedUpdateAll()
     .whenNotMatchedInsertAll()
     .execute())

streaming_df.writeStream.foreachBatch(upsert_to_delta_with_evolution).start()
interview_takeaway: Delta Lake `MERGE INTO` requires `spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled = true` to automatically widen the target table schema during streaming CDC micro-batches without manual DDL intervention.

title: Multi-Tenant Bronze Lakehouse Ingestion with Dynamic Schemas
scenario: A SaaS enterprise ingests telemetry payloads from 5,000 corporate clients into a single Bronze lakehouse table. Each client adds custom JSON properties at will. Attempting to maintain a single merged tabular schema results in a Delta table with over 15,000 columns, causing metastore exhaustion, massive transaction log metadata, and query planning timeouts.
symptom: Driver takes 10+ minutes during query planning phase in Catalyst; Spark UI shows excessive time spent in `Inferring Schema` and `Catalog.getTable()`.
root_cause: Wide schemas with thousands of columns degrade Parquet metadata size and Catalyst optimizer rule application times (quadratic complexity in column resolution).
failing_code:
# Failing Architecture Pattern: Flattening all client schemas into one global table
# Every client's custom properties become physical table columns:
df_client = spark.read.json("s3://tenant-landing/*/*")
df_client.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("bronze.all_tenants")
# Table schema grows to 15,000+ sparse columns! Catalyst planning collapses.
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Semi-Structured Raw Payload + Virtual Tenant Projections
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# 1. Bronze Table Standard: Store invariant metadata + Raw JSON String
# Schema: tenant_id (STRING), event_id (STRING), ingestion_time (TIMESTAMP), raw_payload (STRING)
bronze_df = raw_stream.select(
    F.col("tenant_id"),
    F.col("event_id"),
    F.current_timestamp().alias("ingestion_time"),
    F.col("value").cast("string").alias("raw_payload")
)
bronze_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("bronze.tenant_events")

# 2. Silver/Gold Projection: Project tenant-specific typed schemas using from_json or DBSQL views:
# CREATE VIEW tenant_acme_silver AS
# SELECT tenant_id, event_id, from_json(raw_payload, 'schema_acme') as data
# FROM bronze.tenant_events WHERE tenant_id = 'acme_corp';
interview_takeaway: Never allow multi-tenant dynamic schemas to widen a single physical Delta table into thousands of columns; store semi-structured data as a raw string/variant in Bronze and project strongly typed schemas via tenant-specific views in Silver.

title: Delta Lake Column Mapping and Zero-Copy Renames and Drops
scenario: A 100TB production Delta table requires renaming 5 columns and dropping a deprecated PII column (`ssn`) to comply with GDPR regulations. Prior to Delta Column Mapping, executing `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` required a full rewrite of 100TB of Parquet files, incurring $12,000 in cloud compute and 18 hours of downtime.
symptom: Rewriting entire tables just to rename or drop columns creates massive I/O, cost spikes, and potential transaction conflict aborts.
root_cause: Standard Parquet files store column names in the file footer. Dropping or renaming columns traditionally required reading and rewriting every single Parquet file on storage.
failing_code:
# Legacy Heavyweight Workaround:
# Full Table Rewrite required:
df = spark.read.table("gold.customers").drop("ssn")
df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").saveAsTable("gold.customers_new")
# Rewrites 100TB of data! Expensive and risky.
interview_takeaway: Delta Lake Column Mapping (`delta.columnMapping.mode = 'name'`) decouples logical SQL column names from physical Parquet storage keys, enabling instantaneous, zero-copy column renames and drops without rewriting underlying data files.

title: Malformed CSV Rows with Unescaped Commas and Field Shifts
scenario: A financial data pipeline ingests vendor payment files in CSV format. A vendor name contains an unescaped comma: `"Acme Supplies, Inc."`. Spark reads the row with default CSV settings, splitting the name across two columns and shifting the transaction amount into a date column, causing catastrophic silent data corruption.
symptom: Analytical queries fail with `NumberFormatException` when aggregating the amount column, or revenue figures are corrupted with dates.
root_cause: By default, Spark CSV reader treats commas strictly as delimiters unless explicit quoting rules (`quote`, `escape`) are configured. Unquoted commas shift tokens into adjacent columns.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Data row: 101,Acme Supplies, Inc.,2024-05-01,1500.00
df = spark.read.option("header", "true").csv("s3://vendor/payments.csv")
# Results in:
# id: 101 | name: "Acme Supplies" | address: "Inc." | tx_date: "2024-05-01" | amount: NULL
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Robust Quoting, Escaping, and Schema Validation
df = spark.read \
    .option("header", "true") \
    .option("quote", """) \
    .option("escape", "\\") \
    .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE") \
    .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record") \
    .schema("id INT, vendor_name STRING, tx_date DATE, amount DECIMAL(12,2), _corrupt_record STRING") \
    .csv("s3://vendor/payments.csv")

# Filter out and alert on malformed rows
valid_df = df.filter(F.col("_corrupt_record").isNull()).drop("_corrupt_record")
corrupt_df = df.filter(F.col("_corrupt_record").isNotNull())
interview_takeaway: Never read CSV files without defining an explicit schema and configuring quote/escape delimiters; always capture shifted or malformed records using `columnNameOfCorruptRecord`.

title: JSON Parse Modes: PERMISSIVE vs DROPMALFORMED vs FAILFAST
scenario: An ingestion pipeline uses `mode = 'DROPMALFORMED'` to ingest user feedback JSON files. When a third-party webhook sends 100,000 records with an unclosed bracket `{"user": 12, "comment": ...`, Spark silently drops all 100,000 rows. The team discovers 2 weeks later that 20% of customer feedback was completely lost.
symptom: Job succeeds with status SUCCESS, but total row count drops significantly with zero error traces.
root_cause: `DROPMALFORMED` silently discards any row that fails JSON parsing without notification or logging. In contrast, `FAILFAST` aborts immediately, and `PERMISSIVE` preserves the raw record in a designated corruption column.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# DROPMALFORMED drops bad records into a black hole!
df = spark.read \
    .option("mode", "DROPMALFORMED") \
    .json("s3://webhooks/feedback/")
df.write.format("delta").save("s3://bronze/feedback/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Use PERMISSIVE with _corrupt_record Capture
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, IntegerType

schema = StructType([
    StructField("user_id", IntegerType(), True),
    StructField("comment", StringType(), True),
    StructField("_corrupt_record", StringType(), True)
])

df = spark.read \
    .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE") \
    .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record") \
    .schema(schema) \
    .json("s3://webhooks/feedback/")

# Split valid records from corrupted payloads
valid_df = df.filter(F.col("_corrupt_record").isNull()).drop("_corrupt_record")
corrupt_df = df.filter(F.col("_corrupt_record").isNotNull())

valid_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("bronze.feedback")
corrupt_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("audit.corrupt_feedback")
interview_takeaway: Never use `DROPMALFORMED` in production ingestion pipelines; use `PERMISSIVE` with `columnNameOfCorruptRecord` to safely isolate malformed payloads into an audit quarantine table without data loss.

title: Multi-Line JSON and CSV Split Errors Across Distributed Chunks
scenario: An API exporter writes pretty-printed JSON files (formatted with indentation and newlines across multiple lines). A Spark cluster reads the directory with standard `spark.read.json()`. Tasks fail with `SparkException: Malformed line` or read hundreds of garbage rows consisting of individual JSON property lines.
symptom: Single JSON documents are sliced into fragments across tasks; row counts are 20x higher than expected, with fields showing partial JSON syntax.
root_cause: By default, Spark assumes JSON and CSV are single-line records (one record per line). The reader splits files at arbitrary byte boundaries and expects newline characters to delimit records. For multi-line JSON, `multiLine=true` is required.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Reading multi-line / pretty-printed JSON with single-line assumptions
df = spark.read.json("s3://api-dumps/pretty_printed/*.json")
# Each line '{' or '  "id": 1,' is treated as an individual malformed record!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Enable multiLine and Balance Split Trade-Offs
# Option A: Enable multiLine option
df = spark.read.option("multiLine", "true").json("s3://api-dumps/pretty_printed/*.json")

# PERFORMANCE WARNING: multiLine=true forces Spark to read each file in a single task (non-splittable)
# If files are massive (e.g. 10GB single file), pre-process or convert upstream to newline-delimited JSON (JSONL / NDJSON).

# Option B: Convert upstream to JSON Lines (ndjson) where each complete record is on a single line:
# {"id": 1, "name": "Acme"}
# {"id": 2, "name": "Beta"}
interview_takeaway: Pretty-printed JSON requires `.option('multiLine', 'true')` because Spark defaults to single-line parsing; however, `multiLine=true` disables parallel file splitting, making JSON Lines (`NDJSON`) the preferred enterprise standard.

title: Corrupted Parquet File Footers from Aborted Upstream Writers
scenario: An upstream legacy Spark job killed by an out-of-memory error leaves a partial 0-byte or half-written Parquet file in an unmanaged S3 bucket. Downstream ETL queries reading the directory fail immediately with `IOException: Could not read footer for file`.
symptom: `java.io.IOException: Could not read footer for file: s3://landing/part-00123.parquet` halts the entire enterprise warehouse refresh.
root_cause: Parquet files store essential metadata (schema, row group offsets, dictionary pages) in the file footer at the very end of the file. If a writer is killed midway, the footer is never written, making the physical file unreadable.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Reading raw directory containing half-written Parquet files from aborted job:
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://landing/unmanaged_parquet/")
df.count() # Crashes with IOException: Could not read footer
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Ignore Corrupt Files or Migrate to Delta Lake
# Option 1: Tell Spark to skip corrupt files during emergency batch runs:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.ignoreCorruptFiles", "true")
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://landing/unmanaged_parquet/")

# Option 2: Architectural Solution - Always use Delta Lake or Iceberg!
# Modern lakehouse formats commit files via an atomic transaction log (e.g. _delta_log/).
# A half-written or aborted file is NEVER referenced in the transaction log,
# completely immunizing readers from footer corruption or partial writes.
interview_takeaway: Unmanaged Parquet files are vulnerable to missing footers from interrupted writes; use `spark.sql.files.ignoreCorruptFiles = true` for temporary recovery, and mandate Delta Lake for transactional ACID immunity.

title: Zero-Byte Files and Partial Blocks in Cloud Object Storage
scenario: An SFTP sync script creates zero-byte files (touch markers) while waiting for incoming partner data. When a daily Spark pipeline runs `spark.read.csv()`, tasks throw `EOFException` or `IllegalArgumentException: filePath is empty`.
symptom: Jobs crash during schema inference or initial partition calculation with `java.io.EOFException`.
root_cause: Zero-byte files confuse CSV/JSON schema inferrers and can crash split calculations when metadata exists without readable payload blocks.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# SFTP folder contains: [data_1.csv (10MB), data_2.csv (0 bytes), data_3.csv (0 bytes)]
df = spark.read.option("header", "true").csv("s3://sftp/incoming/*.csv")
# Fails during schema inference on 0-byte file
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Filter Empty Files via Hadoop Path Filter or Auto Loader
# Option 1: Configure Spark to ignore empty/missing files:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.ignoreMissingFiles", "true")

# Option 2: Pre-filter zero-byte paths using JVM Hadoop FileSystem:
sc = spark.sparkContext
conf = sc._jsc.hadoopConfiguration()
Path = sc._gateway.jvm.org.apache.hadoop.fs.Path
fs = Path("s3://sftp/incoming/").getFileSystem(conf)
valid_files = [str(status.getPath()) for status in fs.listStatus(Path("s3://sftp/incoming/")) if status.getLen() > 0]

df = spark.read.option("header", "true").csv(valid_files)

# Option 3: Auto Loader automatically ignores empty files without crashing:
# spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles").option("cloudFiles.format", "csv").load(...)
interview_takeaway: Zero-byte marker files created by ingestion scripts crash schema inference; use Databricks Auto Loader or programmatic Hadoop FileSystem file-length filters to prune 0-byte objects before reading.

title: Safe Isolation of Malformed Records with _corrupt_record
scenario: A health insurance claims pipeline receives JSON claims from 400 hospital networks. Approximately 0.05% of records have invalid JSON syntax (e.g. truncated packets). The business requires 100% processing of valid claims while quarantining invalid claims with full audit tracking.
symptom: Using `FAILFAST` causes 99.95% of legitimate claims to be delayed whenever a single corrupt record arrives.
root_cause: Strict parsing crashes whole micro-batches. Permissive parsing without capturing `_corrupt_record` leaves corrupt records as all-null rows, which contaminate downstream aggregations.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# FAILFAST causes total pipeline blockage
df = spark.read.option("mode", "FAILFAST").json("s3://claims/incoming/")
df.write.format("delta").save("s3://bronze/claims/")
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Dedicated Schema with _corrupt_record Column
from pyspark.sql.types import StructType, StructField, StringType, DoubleType, LongType
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

claims_schema = StructType([
    StructField("claim_id", LongType(), True),
    StructField("patient_id", StringType(), True),
    StructField("claimed_amount", DoubleType(), True),
    StructField("_corrupt_record", StringType(), True) # Must match option name
])

df = spark.read \
    .option("mode", "PERMISSIVE") \
    .option("columnNameOfCorruptRecord", "_corrupt_record") \
    .schema(claims_schema) \
    .json("s3://claims/incoming/")

# 1. Clean Claims Path
clean_claims = df.filter(F.col("_corrupt_record").isNull()).drop("_corrupt_record")
clean_claims.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("silver.claims")

# 2. Quarantine Dead-Letter Path
bad_claims = df.filter(F.col("_corrupt_record").isNotNull()) \
    .withColumn("received_at", F.current_timestamp()) \
    .withColumn("error_reason", F.lit("MALFORMED_JSON_SYNTAX"))

bad_claims.write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("quarantine.corrupt_claims")
interview_takeaway: Include `_corrupt_record` in your declared schema and configure `columnNameOfCorruptRecord` to bifurcate streams into a clean silver table and an auditable quarantine table without stalling the pipeline.

title: Non-UTF-8 Characters and High-Surrogate Code Points in String Functions
scenario: A web scraping pipeline extracts reviews and emoji comments. Upstream scraping bugs write corrupted UTF-16 surrogate pairs or legacy Windows-1252 / ISO-8859-1 byte sequences into Parquet string columns. When running regex extraction or tokenization, Spark tasks fail with `java.nio.charset.MalformedInputException` or JVM string index out-of-bounds.
symptom: `SparkException: Job aborted due to stage failure: java.nio.charset.MalformedInputException: Input length = 1` during regex or string manipulations.
root_cause: The JVM `String` implementation expects valid UTF-16 / UTF-8 sequences. Unpaired high-surrogates or raw binary bytes masquerading as strings violate UTF invariants, breaking JVM string encoders and C++ vectorized execution engines.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Text column contains raw invalid bytes or isolated surrogate characters: '\\uD83D' without low surrogate
df = spark.read.table("raw_reviews")
# Calling regex_replace or substring crashes on invalid surrogate code points
cleaned_df = df.withColumn("cleaned_text", F.regexp_replace("review_text", "[^a-zA-Z0-9 ]", ""))
cleaned_df.count() # Crashes with MalformedInputException
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Sanitize Non-UTF-8 Bytes at Ingestion Boundary
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Option 1: Read binary content and decode with UTF-8 replacement character (U+FFFD)
# In Spark SQL, encode and decode safely:
df_safe = df.withColumn(
    "clean_review_text",
    # Re-encodes string to binary and decodes strictly with replacement:
    F.expr("decode(encode(review_text, 'UTF-8'), 'UTF-8')")
)

# Option 2: Remove high/low surrogate characters using regex range:
# High surrogates: [\\uD800-\\uDBFF], Low surrogates: [\\uDC00-\\uDFFF]
sanitized_df = df.withColumn(
    "sanitized_text",
    F.regexp_replace("review_text", "[\\x00-\\x08\\x0B\\x0C\\x0E-\\x1F\\x7F]", "")
)
interview_takeaway: Corrupt encodings and isolated surrogate code points crash JVM string parsers; sanitize raw strings by re-encoding through UTF-8 or stripping invalid surrogate byte sequences before applying downstream transformations.

title: Auto Loader Rescued Data Column Architecture for Semi-Structured Ingestion
scenario: A gaming telemetry platform ingests 200 million player action events daily. Game client patches frequently alter field casing, rename attributes (e.g. `score` to `player_score`), or submit integers as strings. If the pipeline rejects these files, game telemetry is halted. If it accepts them blindly, the schema corrupts.
symptom: Frequent pipeline halts due to minor client-side format drift.
root_cause: Semi-structured data in production experiences inevitable non-breaking and breaking variations that tabular databases cannot ingest without either strict failure or silent data loss.
failing_code:
# Failing Setup: Rigid Schema Enforcement
streaming_df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") \
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") \
    .schema("player_id STRING, score INT, level INT") \ # Rigid schema
    .load("s3://game/telemetry/")
# If client sends score: "100" (string) or adds new field 'guild_id', score becomes NULL and guild_id is lost!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Auto Loader Rescued Data Pattern
# Auto Loader automatically stores mismatched types, case-mismatches, and undeclared columns in _rescued_data
streaming_df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") \
    .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") \
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaLocation", "s3://lake/checkpoints/game_schema/") \
    .option("cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode", "rescue") \
    .schema("player_id STRING, score INT, level INT") \
    .load("s3://game/telemetry/")

# In Silver processing, inspect _rescued_data for known migrations:
silver_df = streaming_df.withColumn(
    "effective_score",
    F.coalesce(
        F.col("score"),
        F.expr("CAST(_rescued_data['score'] AS INT)"),
        F.expr("CAST(_rescued_data['player_score'] AS INT)")
    )
)
interview_takeaway: Auto Loader's `_rescued_data` column acts as an automated safety net for semi-structured data, capturing type mismatches and undeclared columns so downstream silver pipelines can recover data without ingestion halts.

title: Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) Quarantine Architecture for Kafka Streaming Payloads
scenario: A payments streaming application reads real-time transactions from an Apache Kafka topic. Once every 3 days, a corrupted 'poison pill' packet (e.g. 0-byte payload or invalid Protobuf/Avro bytes) is published to the topic. The Spark Structured Streaming query fails on deserialization and restarts in an infinite retry crash loop.
symptom: Streaming job enters an unrecoverable failure loop (`StreamExecution: query failed with SerializationException`). Real-time SLAs are breached.
root_cause: Structured Streaming checkpoints track Kafka offsets. If the micro-batch cannot deserialize a message at offset $K$, restarting the query causes it to reread offset $K$, hitting the same crash indefinitely.
failing_code:
# Failing Streaming Code:
kafka_stream = spark.readStream.format("kafka") \
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:9092") \
    .option("subscribe", "payments") \
    .load()

# Naive Deserialization in Streaming Plan:
parsed = kafka_stream.select(
    F.from_json(F.col("value").cast("string"), payment_schema).alias("data")
).select("data.*")
# If payload is totally invalid binary, from_json produces all NULLs, or custom UDF deserializer crashes query!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Non-Crashing Deserialization with Offset-Tracked DLQ Egress
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

raw_stream = spark.readStream.format("kafka") \
    .option("kafka.bootstrap.servers", "kafka:9092") \
    .option("subscribe", "payments") \
    .load()

# Step 1: Retain Kafka metadata (topic, partition, offset, timestamp) alongside raw bytes
payload_df = raw_stream.select(
    F.col("topic"),
    F.col("partition"),
    F.col("offset"),
    F.col("timestamp"),
