scenario: A query joins a 10-million row fact table with a 50,000-row dimension table. The developer accidentally writes `FROM sales, stores` without a `WHERE sales.store_id = stores.store_id` predicate. The query attempts to generate $10,000,000 \times 50,000 = 500,000,000,000$ (500 billion) rows, crashing the cluster.
symptom: `AnalysisException: Detected implicit cartesian product for INNER join between logical plans... Use the CROSS JOIN syntax to allow cartesian products` or executor disk fill-up.
root_cause: Omitting a join condition creates a Cartesian product where every row of the left table joins with every row of the right table.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
-- Omitted join predicate:
SELECT *
FROM sales_fact, store_dim; -- Cartesian explosion!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Explicit ANSI JOIN Syntax with Equi-Join Predicate
SELECT *
FROM sales_fact s
INNER JOIN store_dim d ON s.store_id = d.store_id;

-- Best Practice: Never use legacy comma-separated table syntax ('FROM a, b').
-- Enforce spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled = false in cluster configuration so that
-- accidental Cartesian products fail immediately during query planning rather than wasting compute!
interview_takeaway: Legacy comma-separated joins easily cause accidental Cartesian explosions; always use explicit ANSI `INNER JOIN ... ON` syntax and set `spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled = false` to intercept missing join keys during planning.

title: Many-to-Many Join Multiplying Fact Row Counts Silently
scenario: An analytics query joins an `orders` table (1M rows) with a `customer_addresses` table. Because customers have multiple historical shipping addresses, each order joins with an average of 4 addresses. The output row count explodes from 1 million to 4 million, quadrupling the reported order revenue in the executive BI report.
symptom: Analytical BI reports show revenue inflated by 400%; financial reconciliation audits fail.
root_cause: A 1:N or N:M relationship in what was assumed to be a 1:1 dimension lookup multiplies matching fact rows.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
orders = spark.read.table("gold.orders")             # 1M rows
addresses = spark.read.table("silver.addresses")     # Has 4 addresses per customer!

# Many-to-many join explosion:
exploded_orders = orders.join(addresses, on="customer_id", how="inner")
print(exploded_orders.count()) # 4M rows! Revenue is 4x too high!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Filter to Active / Default Dimension Entity Pre-Join
# Filter dimension to exactly 1 row per entity (e.g. current default address):
current_addresses = addresses.filter(F.col("is_default_shipping") == True)

# Safe 1:1 join:
clean_orders = orders.join(current_addresses, on="customer_id", how="inner")

# Automated Pipeline Test Assertion:
# assert clean_orders.count() == orders.count(), "INTEGRITY VIOLATION: Join multiplied fact rows!"
interview_takeaway: Joining facts with multi-record dimensions silently multiplies financial metrics; filter dimensions to unique primary keys (e.g. `is_current = true`) before joining and assert that row counts do not expand.

title: Inadvertent Full Outer Join Exploding Table Size on Non-Matching Keys
scenario: A data integration pipeline combines clickstream events from Web and Mobile apps. An engineer attempts to unify them using `FULL OUTER JOIN` on `session_id`. However, web and mobile apps generate completely disjoint session ID schemes (`web_xxx` vs `mob_yyy`). The join produces 0 matches, outputting a massive sparse table containing 100% NULLs on opposite sides.
symptom: Table size doubles; output contains billions of rows that are 50% NULL.
root_cause: Full Outer Join preserves all rows from both tables. When join keys are disjoint (0 overlap), `FULL OUTER JOIN` degenerates into a row union with double the width and full null-padding.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
-- Web and mobile have disjoint session IDs:
SELECT *
FROM web_clicks w
FULL OUTER JOIN mobile_clicks m ON w.session_id = m.session_id;
-- 0 matches! Generates 100M + 100M = 200M rows with 50% NULL columns!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: UnionByName for Disjoint Datasets
-- When unifying disjoint sources representing the same logical entity, use UNION ALL / unionByName:
SELECT 'WEB' AS platform, session_id, url AS page, event_time FROM web_clicks
UNION ALL
SELECT 'MOBILE' AS platform, session_id, screen_name AS page, event_time FROM mobile_clicks;

-- In PySpark:
# df_web.select("session_id", "page", "event_time").unionByName(df_mob.select("session_id", "page", "event_time"))
interview_takeaway: Do not use `FULL OUTER JOIN` to merge disparate event streams sharing no common join keys; use `UNION ALL` or `unionByName()` to stack schemas vertically without creating sparse null-padded Cartesian row overhead.

title: Non-Equi Join Performance Collapse and Cartesian Fallback
scenario: A currency exchange pipeline converts transaction amounts using an exchange rates table that changes daily. The join condition is written as: `ON tx.currency = fx.currency AND tx.tx_time >= fx.valid_from AND tx.tx_time < fx.valid_to`. Catalyst cannot use a Hash or SortMergeJoin due to the inequalities, and query runtime balloons from 3 minutes to 4 hours.
symptom: Spark UI shows physical plan `CartesianProduct` or `SortMergeJoin` with massive residual filter time; execution is painfully slow.
root_cause: Hash joins and SortMergeJoins require at least one equi-join predicate (`a = b`). Pure range or inequality conditions prevent hash-based bucketing, forcing Catalyst to perform quadratic $O(M \times N)$ comparisons.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
SELECT tx.*, fx.rate * tx.amount AS usd_amount
FROM transactions tx
JOIN exchange_rates fx
    ON tx.currency = fx.currency
    AND tx.tx_timestamp >= fx.valid_from
    AND tx.tx_timestamp < fx.valid_to; -- Non-equi range check!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Discrete Date-Key Equi-Join Pre-Expansion
-- Step 1: Pre-join or expand FX rates to discrete daily calendar dates:
-- Create a daily fx lookup: (currency, date, rate)

-- Step 2: Rewrite join with an exact equi-join on BOTH currency AND date:
SELECT tx.*, fx.rate * tx.amount AS usd_amount
FROM transactions tx
JOIN exchange_rates_daily fx
    ON tx.currency = fx.currency
    AND to_date(tx.tx_timestamp) = fx.rate_date; -- Pure Equi-Join!

-- Catalyst now uses high-speed BroadcastHashJoin or SortMergeJoin (runs in 45 seconds)!
interview_takeaway: Catalyst cannot hash-partition on inequality predicates; convert continuous range conditions into discrete calendar date equi-joins (`to_date(event_time) = fx.date`) to unlock high-speed SortMerge or BroadcastHash joins.

title: Range Join Optimization for Point-in-Interval IP-to-Country Lookups
scenario: A cybersecurity pipeline resolves 100 million client IP addresses to geographic countries using a MaxMind GeoIP database containing 4 million CIDR ranges: `WHERE client_ip_num BETWEEN range_start AND range_end`. The query triggers a Cartesian join and runs out of memory.
symptom: Job fails with `OutOfMemoryError` or runs for hours with 0 progress in `CartesianProductExec`.
root_cause: Point-in-interval queries (`A BETWEEN start AND end`) are non-equi joins. Without an exact equality key, Spark must test every IP against all 4 million IP blocks.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
SELECT l.ip_string, g.country_code
FROM web_logs l
JOIN geo_ip_ranges g
    ON l.ip_numeric >= g.start_ip
    AND l.ip_numeric <= g.end_ip; -- Triggers Cartesian Product!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Range-Binning Equi-Join Optimization
-- Step 1: Deconstruct IP addresses into 16-bit prefix bins (Class B / /16 blocks = 65,536 bins)
-- Add bin_id = floor(ip_numeric / 65536) to both logs and IP ranges

-- Step 2: Expand geo ranges that span multiple bins using explode(sequence(start_bin, end_bin))
-- Step 3: Join on the equi-key bin_id FIRST, then apply residual range filter:
SELECT l.ip_string, g.country_code
FROM (
    SELECT *, floor(ip_numeric / 65536) AS ip_bin FROM web_logs
) l
JOIN geo_ranges_binned g
    ON l.ip_bin = g.range_bin -- EQUI-JOIN eliminates 99.99% of candidates!
    AND l.ip_numeric >= g.start_ip
    AND l.ip_numeric <= g.end_ip;

-- In Databricks, native Range Join Optimization can also be enabled:
-- spark.conf.set("spark.databricks.optimizer.rangeJoin.enabled", "true")
interview_takeaway: Optimize point-in-interval range joins by discretizing ranges into coarse equi-join hash bins (e.g. 16-bit prefix bins) to eliminate 99.9% of candidate pairs before evaluating the inequality.

title: Semi Join vs Inner Join + Distinct Performance Differential
scenario: A marketing pipeline finds all customers who made a purchase in the last 30 days. The developer writes: `SELECT DISTINCT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id`. With 200 million orders and 10 million customers, the join creates 150 million intermediate rows and forces a massive distributed distinct shuffle.
symptom: Stage spills 120GB to disk during the `DISTINCT` aggregation phase after the join.
root_cause: `INNER JOIN` multiplies customer rows for every matching order, and `DISTINCT` must then deduplicate all columns across the network. A `LEFT SEMI JOIN` stops scanning the right table as soon as the first match is found, emitting each customer at most once without duplication.
failing_code:
-- Inefficient Anti-Pattern: Inner Join + Distinct
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id, c.name, c.email, c.tier
FROM customers c
INNER JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id; -- Multiplies rows, forces heavy DISTINCT shuffle!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: LEFT SEMI JOIN (Zero Row Multiplication!)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.email, c.tier
FROM customers c
LEFT SEMI JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id;

-- In PySpark:
# customers.join(orders, on="customer_id", how="left_semi")

-- Catalyst short-circuits on first order match per customer.
-- 0 row multiplication, 0 intermediate duplicate rows, 0 DISTINCT shuffle! 5x faster!
interview_takeaway: Never use `INNER JOIN` + `DISTINCT` when filtering for entity existence; use `LEFT SEMI JOIN` to short-circuit on the first match, preventing row multiplication and eliminating expensive distinct shuffles.

title: Anti Join with NULL Keys Silently Discarding Records
scenario: A churn analysis query identifies inactive users who have not logged in for 90 days. The query is written as: `WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM logins_90d)`. A single test user record has `user_id = NULL` in `logins_90d`. The query returns 0 churned users.
symptom: Zero results returned in production without syntax or schema errors.
root_cause: Under SQL ANSI 3-valued logic, `x NOT IN (..., NULL)` is UNKNOWN. A `LEFT ANTI JOIN` avoids this trap because it operates on equality semantics rather than subquery value set expansion.
failing_code:
-- Failing Subquery Pattern:
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM logins_90d); -- Single NULL kills entire query!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: LEFT ANTI JOIN
SELECT u.*
FROM users u
LEFT ANTI JOIN logins_90d l ON u.user_id = l.user_id;

-- In PySpark:
# inactive_users = users.join(logins_90d, on="user_id", how="left_anti")

-- Left Anti Join guarantees correct exclusion regardless of NULLs on either side!
interview_takeaway: `NOT IN` collapses to empty when the target subquery contains NULLs; use `LEFT ANTI JOIN` in Spark to guarantee accurate entity exclusion and optimal Catalyst join planning.

title: Join Order Optimization Collapse in Multi-Table Snowflake Queries
scenario: An enterprise reporting query joins 7 tables: 1 massive fact table (5 billion rows) and 6 dimension tables. Catalyst generates an execution plan that joins the 5-billion-row fact table with a large dimension first, generating a 20-billion-row intermediate shuffle, instead of filtering small dimensions first.
symptom: Query takes 3 hours. Spark UI shows intermediate shuffle stages handling billions of unneeded records.
root_cause: Spark Cost-Based Optimizer (CBO) is disabled by default (`spark.sql.cbo.enabled = false`) or lacks accurate table/column statistics. Without statistics, Catalyst evaluates joins in left-to-right syntactic order or uses simple heuristics, picking suboptimal join trees.
failing_code:
# Failing Setup: CBO disabled, missing statistics
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.cbo.enabled", "false")

# 7-table join executed in naive order:
df = fact.join(dim1, "k1").join(dim2, "k2").join(dim3, "k3").join(dim4, "k4")...
interview_takeaway: Catalyst can make disastrous join order decisions in multi-table queries without metadata; enable Cost-Based Optimizer (`spark.sql.cbo.enabled = true`) and run `ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS` to let Spark find the optimal join tree.

title: Dynamic Partition Pruning (DPP) Failure on Non-Broadcast Star Joins
scenario: A 100TB fact table is partitioned by `date_key`. A BI query joins `fact_sales` with `dim_date` filtering for `quarter = 'Q3'`. Instead of reading only Q3 partitions (25TB), Spark reads all 100TB from cloud storage, exhausting cluster budget.
symptom: Spark UI shows 100% of partition files read; `DynamicPartitionPruning` operator is absent from the physical execution plan.
root_cause: Dynamic Partition Pruning (DPP) relies on the dimension table being broadcast. If `dim_date` exceeds the broadcast threshold or if the join is forced into a SortMergeJoin, DPP cannot inject runtime partition filters into the fact table scan.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
-- dim_date has 50 columns and exceeds autoBroadcastJoinThreshold:
SELECT f.*
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
WHERE d.quarter = 'Q3'; -- Scans ALL 100TB of fact partitions because DPP was not triggered!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Force Broadcast Hint on Dimension to Trigger DPP
-- Option 1: Broadcast the dimension to activate Dynamic Partition Pruning:
SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(d) */ f.*
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d ON f.date_key = d.date_key
WHERE d.quarter = 'Q3';

-- In Physical Plan, look for:
-- "DynamicPruningExpression(date_key#123 IN dynamicpruning#456)"
-- Spark now skips 75TB of partitions at runtime during the initial storage scan!

-- Option 2: Ensure DPP configuration is active:
-- SET spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.enabled = true;
-- SET spark.sql.optimizer.dynamicPartitionPruning.useStats = true;
interview_takeaway: Dynamic Partition Pruning (DPP) skips irrelevant fact table partitions at runtime based on dimension filters, but DPP requires the dimension side to be broadcast; use `/*+ BROADCAST */` hints on the filtering dimension to guarantee DPP activation.

title: Enterprise Fact-Dimension Join Optimization: Runtime Bloom Filter Joins
scenario: A lakehouse fact table of 10 billion rows cannot be broadcast, nor can the filtered dimension (50 million rows). Both tables must shuffle. Even with 1,000 partitions, the shuffle exchange transfers 8TB across the network. 80% of fact records will ultimately be discarded by the join.
symptom: Massive shuffle read/write metrics; 80% of shuffled data is immediately dropped post-join.
root_cause: SortMergeJoin shuffles all rows from both tables before filtering non-matching keys. If most fact rows have no match in the filtered dimension, massive network bandwidth is wasted shuffling doomed rows.
failing_code:
# Standard SortMergeJoin without pre-filtering:
# 8TB fact table shuffled across network, only to discard 80% post-join!
joined = fact_sales.join(filtered_dim, on="customer_id")
joined.write.format("delta").save(...)
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Runtime Bloom Filter Join (Databricks / Spark 3.3+)
# Step 1: Enable Bloom Filter Join Optimization:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.creationSideThreshold", "100MB")

# How it works internally:
# 1. Spark builds a probabilistic Bloom Filter (tiny bitset, ~10MB) from filtered_dim keys on Driver.
# 2. Spark pushes down the Bloom Filter to the fact_sales scan tasks.
# 3. Fact scanner evaluates the Bloom Filter at the Parquet reader level, discarding 80% of rows
#    BEFORE they are ever read into memory or sent to the shuffle buffer!
# 4. Shuffle data drops from 8TB to 1.6TB! 5x faster execution!
interview_takeaway: Runtime Bloom Filter Joins (`spark.sql.optimizer.runtime.bloomFilter.enabled = true`) build an in-memory bitset from the dimension to prune non-matching fact rows at the Parquet scan level, slashing shuffle network traffic by up to 80%.

title: Floating-Point Imprecision in Financial Currency Calculations
scenario: A payments reconciliation pipeline calculates merchant balances by summing transaction fees stored as `DoubleType`. Adding fees of $0.10 and $0.20 yields $0.30000000000000004. Over millions of transactions, balance audits fail by thousands of dollars due to floating-point rounding accumulation.
symptom: Balance sheets fail exact zero-sum reconciliation audits; pennies drift across ledger accounts.
root_cause: IEEE 754 floating-point numbers (`FloatType`, `DoubleType`) represent base-10 fractional decimals in binary base-2, creating inherent binary rounding approximations.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# Storing monetary values as DoubleType:
df = spark.createDataFrame([(0.10,), (0.20,)], ["fee"])
result = df.agg(F.sum("fee")).collect()[0][0]
print(result) # 0.30000000000000004 (NOT 0.30!)
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Use Fixed-Point DecimalType(18, 4) or DecimalType(38, 2)
from pyspark.sql.types import DecimalType
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Cast or declare financial fields as DecimalType:
df_decimal = df.withColumn("fee", F.col("fee").cast(DecimalType(18, 4)))

result = df_decimal.agg(F.sum("fee")).collect()[0][0]
print(result) # Decimal('0.3000') - Exact, deterministic mathematical precision!

# In Spark DDL:
# CREATE TABLE ledger (tx_id STRING, amount DECIMAL(18, 2)) USING DELTA;
interview_takeaway: Never use `DoubleType` or `FloatType` for currency or monetary accounting; always use `DecimalType(precision, scale)` to avoid IEEE 754 binary floating-point drift.

title: Silent Integer Overflow in Spark 3.x vs spark.sql.ansi.enabled
scenario: A telecommunications company calculates total bandwidth usage in bytes across subscribers using `IntegerType`. When total usage exceeds $2,147,483,647$ ($2^{31}-1$), the sum wraps into negative numbers (`-2,147,483,400`), resulting in negative customer bills.
symptom: Aggregated metrics suddenly turn negative without throwing any arithmetic exceptions or warnings.
root_cause: By default in non-ANSI mode (`spark.sql.ansi.enabled = false`), integer arithmetic overflow wraps around based on standard two's-complement binary arithmetic rather than failing or promoting to BIGINT.
failing_code:
# Failing Non-ANSI Setup:
# Integer max is 2,147,483,647
df = spark.createDataFrame([(2147483640,), (100,)], ["bytes_used"]) # IntegerType
df.agg(F.sum("bytes_used")).show()
# Returns: -2147483556 ! Silent numeric corruption!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Enable ANSI Mode or Cast to BIGINT / Decimal
# Option A: Cast to LongType (BIGINT) before aggregating:
df_safe = df.withColumn("bytes_used", F.col("bytes_used").cast("bigint"))
df_safe.agg(F.sum("bytes_used")).show() # Correct: 2147483740

# Option B: Enable ANSI SQL compliance (Spark 3.0+ / Default in Spark 4.0):
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.ansi.enabled", "true")
# When overflow occurs, Spark immediately throws ArithmeticException: integer overflow,
# preventing negative numbers from corrupting production tables!
interview_takeaway: Non-ANSI Spark wraps integer overflows silently into negative numbers; protect pipelines by casting accumulation columns to `BIGINT` and enabling `spark.sql.ansi.enabled = true`.

title: Decimal Precision and Scale Truncation in Multi-Step Calculations
scenario: A bond pricing pipeline performs repeated compound interest calculations on `DECIMAL(38, 18)` numbers. When multiplying two high-precision decimals, Spark SQL truncates fractional digits, turning numbers like `0.000000000000123456` into `0.000000`, causing bond yield calculations to round to zero.
symptom: Fractional decimals lose precision and round down to zero during multiplication or division chains.
root_cause: Spark SQL enforces a maximum decimal precision of 38 digits. When multiplying `DECIMAL(p1, s1)` and `DECIMAL(p2, s2)`, result precision is $p1 + p2 + 1$. Because precision cannot exceed 38, Spark caps precision at 38 and trims the scale ($s$), sacrificing fractional digits.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
-- Decimal multiplication capping at 38 precision:
SELECT CAST(1.000000000000000001 AS DECIMAL(38, 18)) * 
       CAST(0.000000000000000001 AS DECIMAL(38, 18)) AS result;
-- Truncates scale, returning 0.000000!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Right-Size Precision or Use Double for Scientific Chains
-- Rule: Do not declare arbitrary DECIMAL(38, 18) when unnecessary!
-- Size precision and scale to the minimum required:
SELECT CAST(1.000001 AS DECIMAL(14, 6)) * CAST(0.000001 AS DECIMAL(14, 6)) AS result;
-- Result precision = 29 <= 38, scale is 100% preserved without truncation!

-- In PySpark, tune decimal loss of precision policy:
-- spark.conf.set("spark.sql.decimalOperations.allowPrecisionLoss", "false")
-- Throws an exception if precision loss would occur rather than silently rounding to zero!
interview_takeaway: Spark decimals cap at 38 precision; multiplying two `DECIMAL(38, 18)` numbers forces scale reduction and fractional truncation. Right-size precision (e.g. `DECIMAL(18, 6)`) and set `allowPrecisionLoss = false`.

title: Implicit String-to-Numeric Casting Preventing Partition Pruning
scenario: A 50TB partitioned lakehouse table is physically partitioned by `date_key STRING` (e.g. `'20241031'`). A user queries `WHERE date_key = 20241031` (integer literal). Catalyst evaluates the predicate by applying `CAST(date_key AS INT)` to every single partition, disabling directory pruning and scanning all 50TB.
symptom: Query scans 100% of physical storage; execution time increases from 2 seconds to 25 minutes.
root_cause: When comparing a String column to an Integer literal, type precedence rules dictate that the String column must be cast to Integer: `CAST(date_key AS INT) = 20241031`. Because the partition column is wrapped in a function, it is non-sargable, preventing storage partition pruning.
failing_code:
-- Failing Spark SQL:
-- Table partitioned by date_key STRING ('20241031')
SELECT *
FROM fact_sales
WHERE date_key = 20241031; -- Integer literal! Forces full table scan of 50TB!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Sargable Matching Predicate Types
-- Always match the exact datatype of the partition column:
SELECT *
FROM fact_sales
WHERE date_key = '20241031'; -- String literal! 

-- Catalyst immediately matches partition path 'date_key=20241031' and reads only 500MB!

-- In PySpark:
# df.filter(F.col("date_key") == F.lit("20241031")) # Explicit string literal
interview_takeaway: Passing numeric literals to string partition columns wraps the column in an implicit `CAST()`, destroying partition pruning and forcing a full table scan; always match filter literal types to partition schema types.

title: Lexicographical String Ordering Bug in Date Comparisons
scenario: A reporting query filters for events after September 1st using string comparison: `WHERE event_date > '2024-9-1'`. Because dates were unpadded strings, the comparison `'2024-10-01' > '2024-9-1'` evaluates to FALSE in lexicographical ASCII comparison. All October and November records are excluded from Q4 reports.
symptom: October and November data is missing from Q4 revenue calculations.
root_cause: In ASCII string comparison, character `'1'` has a lower ordinal value than `'9'`. Therefore, string `'2024-10-01'` is lexicographically smaller than `'2024-9-1'`.
failing_code:
-- Failing String Comparison:
SELECT *
FROM audit_logs
WHERE date_str > '2024-9-1';
-- '2024-10-01' > '2024-9-1' evaluates to FALSE! Omits entire month of October!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: Use Strongly Typed Date/Timestamp Types
-- Always cast strings to DATE or TIMESTAMP for chronological comparisons:
SELECT *
FROM audit_logs
WHERE to_date(date_str, 'yyyy-M-d') > DATE '2024-09-01';

-- Best Practice: In lakehouse schemas, never store dates as raw unstructured strings.
-- Always declare them as DateType or TimestampNTZType with ISO-8601 formatting ('yyyy-MM-dd').
interview_takeaway: String date comparisons follow ASCII alphabetical rules where `'2024-10'` is less than `'2024-9'`; always cast to `DateType` or enforce zero-padded ISO-8601 formatting (`'2024-09-01'`) for date filters.

title: Unicode Normalization Form Mismatch Breaking String Joins
scenario: A European customer master table joins identity records from an iOS app and a Windows legacy database on `customer_name`. The name `'Renée'` fails to match across systems. Visually the strings appear identical, but the join drops 8% of European customers.
symptom: Identical-looking text fails string equality checks and join conditions.
root_cause: Unicode allows characters with accents to be represented in two forms: NFC (Canonical Decomposition followed by Canonical Composition: single code point `U+00E9`) and NFD (Canonical Decomposition: base letter `e` + combining acute accent `U+0301`). In binary string comparison, NFC and NFD strings have different byte sequences.
failing_code:
# Failing PySpark Code:
# iOS writes NFD ('Rene\u0301e'), Windows writes NFC ('Ren\u00e9e')
df_ios = spark.createDataFrame([("Rene\u0301e",)], ["name"])
df_win = spark.createDataFrame([("Ren\u00e9e",)], ["name"])

joined = df_ios.join(df_win, on="name")
print(joined.count()) # Returns 0 matches!
interview_takeaway: Visually identical international strings fail joins when encoded in different Unicode forms (NFC vs NFD); normalize all text columns using `normalize(col, 'NFC')` during bronze ingestion.

title: Parquet INT96 Deprecation and Nanosecond Timestamp Shifts
scenario: A legacy Hive/Impala pipeline wrote Parquet files using the legacy `INT96` timestamp format. When migrating to Spark 3.x with modern Parquet readers, timestamps shift by hundreds of years (e.g. year 1870) or fail with `IllegalArgumentException: Parquet INT96 is deprecated`.
symptom: Timestamps show bizarre dates (years 1870 or 2060) or query fails with INT96 rebasing exceptions.
root_cause: Legacy Hive used INT96 (12 bytes) for timestamps without timezone metadata, based on the Julian calendar. Modern Spark 3.0+ uses INT64 with Gregorian calendar rebasing (`spark.sql.parquet.datetimeRebaseModeInRead`).
failing_code:
# Failing Spark 3.x Parquet Read:
# Reading legacy INT96 Parquet table:
df = spark.read.parquet("s3://legacy/hive_int96_table/")
# Fails with SparkUpgradeException: You may see a different result from Spark 2.4 because 
# Spark 3.0 uses the Proleptic Gregorian calendar...
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Configure Parquet Rebase Mode & Modern Output Types
# Step 1: For reading legacy INT96 files safely in Spark 3.x:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.datetimeRebaseModeInRead", "LEGACY")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInRead", "LEGACY")

# Step 2: For writing modern, standard-compliant Parquet / Delta files:
# Configure output format to INT64 TIMESTAMP_MICROS (Standard Parquet format):
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.parquet.outputTimestampType", "TIMESTAMP_MICROS")

# Step 3: Permanently rewrite legacy tables to modern Delta format to eliminate INT96 forever.
interview_takeaway: Legacy Hive Parquet tables used deprecated INT96 Julian timestamps; set `spark.sql.parquet.int96RebaseModeInRead = 'LEGACY'` to read them safely, and standardize writes on INT64 `TIMESTAMP_MICROS` in Delta Lake.

title: Binary Serialization Header Shifts in Kafka Avro and Protobuf Streams
scenario: A streaming ingestion pipeline parses Confluent Kafka Avro payloads using `from_avro()`. Deserialization throws `AvroRuntimeException: Not an Avro file` on every single record, failing the streaming pipeline.
symptom: `org.apache.avro.AvroRuntimeException: Not an Avro data file` on valid Kafka messages.
root_cause: Confluent Schema Registry prepends a 5-byte wire protocol header to every Kafka message (Magic Byte 0x00 + 4-byte Schema ID). Standard Apache Avro readers expect the raw binary payload; the extra 5-byte header breaks the Avro magic number parser.
failing_code:
# Failing Streaming Code:
# Standard from_avro on Confluent wire format:
stream_df = spark.readStream.format("kafka").load()
# Fails because bytes 0-4 are Schema Registry metadata, not Avro record body:
parsed = stream_df.select(F.from_avro("value", avro_schema).alias("data"))
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Strip 5-Byte Confluent Header or Use Schema Registry Provider
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Option A: Strip the 5-byte Confluent header using substring:
# In PySpark, substring on binary operates on 1-based byte index:
# Byte 1: Magic byte (0x00)
# Bytes 2-5: Schema ID (4 bytes)
# Bytes 6+: Real Avro binary body!
clean_binary = stream_df.withColumn(
    "avro_body",
    F.expr("substring(value, 6, length(value) - 5)")
)
parsed = clean_binary.select(F.from_avro("avro_body", avro_schema).alias("data"))

# Option B: Use Databricks Confluent Schema Registry Native Integration:
# from_avro("value", schemaRegistryAddress="http://registry:8081") (automatically handles header!)
interview_takeaway: Confluent Avro streams prepend a 5-byte wire-format header to Kafka messages; strip bytes 1-5 via `substring(value, 6)` before calling `from_avro()`, or configure native Schema Registry integration.

title: Cross-Platform Float and NaN Serialization Discrepancies
scenario: A machine learning feature store computes aggregations in PySpark, exports them to Parquet, and reads them with Python Pandas. In Pandas, `NaN` values in integer columns force the entire column to cast to `float64`. Downstream feature lookups on customer IDs like `1042.0` fail to match integer `1042`.
symptom: Model training features fail join lookups in production Python services due to `.0` float suffix.
root_cause: Legacy Pandas uses IEEE 754 `NaN` (float) to represent missing values in numeric series. When reading Parquet files with nullable integer columns, older Pandas runtimes automatically promote the integer column to `float64`.
failing_code:
# Incompatible Workflow:
# PySpark writes nullable Integer: [1001, 1002, NULL]
df_spark.write.parquet("s3://features/customer_ids/")

# In Python service:
pdf = pd.read_parquet("s3://features/customer_ids/")
print(pdf["customer_id"].dtype) # float64! Values are [1001.0, 1002.0, NaN]
# Lookup on '1001' fails because Pandas holds 1001.0!
solution_code:
# Production-Grade Solution: Enforce Int64 Extension Array or Fill Imputation
# Option A: In Pandas 1.0+, use nullable Integer extension type 'Int64':
import pandas as pd
pdf = pd.read_parquet("s3://features/customer_ids/")
pdf["customer_id"] = pdf["customer_id"].astype("Int64") # Preserves integer representation with pd.NA!

# Option B: In PySpark, eliminate NULLs on primary keys prior to export:
df_clean = df_spark.filter(F.col("customer_id").isNotNull())

# Option C: Use string representation for high-precision entity identifiers:
df_spark = df_spark.withColumn("customer_id", F.col("customer_id").cast("string"))
interview_takeaway: Legacy Pandas casts nullable integers to `float64` to accommodate `NaN`, causing ID corruption; store primary identifiers as `StringType` or enforce Pandas `Int64` nullable integer extension types across the ML serving boundary.

title: Schema Evolution Type Narrowing Lockouts & ANSI SQL Compliance Migration
scenario: An enterprise lakehouse with 500 pipelines migrates from Spark 2.4 to Spark 3.4 with ANSI SQL compliance (`spark.sql.ansi.enabled = true`). Over 100 batch pipelines fail on day one with `ArithmeticException: overflow`, `DateTimeParseException`, and `AnalysisException: Cannot cast STRING to BIGINT safely`. The team considers disabling ANSI mode, sacrificing data quality.
symptom: Massive pipeline failures across production after Spark runtime upgrade; jobs fail on strict casting rules.
root_cause: Spark 3+ ANSI mode changes default behavior from lenient (where overflows return NULL and bad casts return NULL) to strict standard SQL (which throws exceptions on invalid casts or overflows).
failing_code:
# Legacy Pipeline Code that crashes under ANSI mode:
# 'abc' is not a number; under non-ANSI, cast returns NULL. Under ANSI mode, it crashes!
df.select(F.col("raw_token").cast("bigint")).show()
# Crashes with NumberFormatException: For input string: "abc"!
solution_code:
-- Production-Grade Solution: ANSI SQL Migration Strategy using TRY_ Functions
-- Step 1: Migrate brittle CAST expressions to ANSI-compliant TRY_CAST / TRY_TO_NUMBER:
-- TRY_CAST returns NULL on invalid conversion without crashing the query!
SELECT TRY_CAST(raw_token AS BIGINT) AS safe_token
FROM raw_logs;

-- Step 2: Use TRY_ADD, TRY_MULTIPLY, TRY_DIVIDE for safe arithmetic:
SELECT TRY_DIVIDE(numerator, denominator) AS safe_ratio
FROM metrics;

-- Step 3: For timestamps, use TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP:
SELECT TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP(raw_date, 'yyyy-MM-dd') AS safe_date
FROM raw_logs;

-- Result: Full ANSI compliance, zero pipeline crash risk, clean nullification of corrupt inputs!
interview_takeaway: When migrating to ANSI SQL compliance in Spark 3.x/4.x, replace standard `CAST()` and arithmetic operators with `TRY_CAST()`, `TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP()`, and `TRY_DIVIDE()` to preserve fault-tolerant NULL semantics on malformed inputs.
